title: Pediatric Urology Fellowships
prerequisites: Prior physician education and completed/near-completed urology residency for intended fellowship-level learner; not a stand-alone path into medicine
Prerequisite experience in pediatric anatomy, embryology, general urology, pediatric assessment and evidence-based medicine.
objectives: Integrate age-specific pediatric GU anatomy, developmental origins, imaging and pathophysiology into safe differential diagnosis.
Map symptoms and findings to risk-aware evaluation plans while identifying emergencies, DSD/neurologic red flags and need for multidisciplinary care.
Compare guideline-supported surveillance, preventive and reconstructive concepts without treating any single source, image or case report as determinative.
Interpret urologic studies and published evidence with attention to uncertainty, age, long-term outcomes, ethics, privacy and transition.
Explain ABU board structure, public-programme limits and boundaries of independent self-study.

units.title: Developmental anatomy, fetal evaluation, CAKUT and prenatal counseling
objectives: Trace clinically relevant renal, ureteral, bladder and genital development and connect developmental errors to common anomalies.
Differentiate antenatal urinary-tract dilation, lower urinary-tract obstruction and urgent fetal/neonatal risk features; formulate a differential rather than a premature label.
Describe multidisciplinary counseling, uncertainty and limits of fetal intervention evidence.
topics: Embryology and renal/ureteric development; CAKUT; prenatal UTD risk stratification; posterior urethral valves and fetal lower urinary-tract obstruction; fetal/neonatal evaluation; genetics and family counseling.
units.casePractice: Read the linked fetal stone/UPJ obstruction case; present prenatal differential and postnatal follow-up questions without assuming one case dictates practice.
units.assessment: One-page fetal UTD / suspected LUTO differential and a short caregiver-facing explanation that separates screening result from diagnosis.

units.title: Upper-tract dilation, obstruction, ureteral anomalies and functional imaging
objectives: Interpret ultrasound and diuretic renography conceptually, including limits of each measure.
Compare observation, additional assessment and intervention as evidence-sensitive options for upper-tract dilation.
Differentiate ureterocele, ectopic ureter, duplex systems, megaureter and UPJ obstruction.
topics: Antenatal/postnatal UTD; hydronephrosis classification; UPJ obstruction; megaureter; duplication; ureterocele/ectopic ureter; diuresis renography; renal outcome endpoints.
units.casePractice: Use a public case-report link to frame differential for prenatal hydronephrosis; no images downloaded or patient-specific conclusions.
units.assessment: Interpret a fictional serial imaging vignette and state what additional clinical context is required before choosing follow-up.

units.title: UTI, pyelonephritis, VUR and renal risk
objectives: Build a risk-based history, physical and diagnostic approach for pediatric febrile UTI and known/suspected reflux.
Explain how age, febrile infections, renal findings and bladder-bowel dysfunction inform risk and follow-up.
Compare observation, prophylaxis and intervention as options requiring family-centred decisions and updated local guidance.
topics: Urine culture quality; febrile UTI; pyelonephritis; VUR grade and natural history; renal ultrasound/DMSA roles; continuous antibiotic prophylaxis evidence; BBD; recurrence prevention; follow-up.
units.casePractice: Compare an authentic open case report with a fictional febrile-UTI vignette; explicitly identify where a single case cannot estimate treatment effect.
units.assessment: Write a short evidence table distinguishing guideline recommendation, option, and evidence uncertainty; use guideline date labels.

units.title: Daytime LUT dysfunction, enuresis, bowel-bladder dysfunction and urodynamics
objectives: Use a voiding/bowel history and diary to distinguish storage, emptying and bowel-related symptoms.
Identify red flags suggesting obstruction or neurologic disease that warrant escalation beyond uncomplicated functional symptoms.
Interpret uroflow/PVR and urodynamic concepts without overreading a single test.
topics: Voiding diary; daytime incontinence; dysfunctional voiding; constipation; enuresis; urotherapy concepts; uroflowmetry; post-void residual; urodynamics indications; psychosocial impact.
units.casePractice: Review an open access LUTD paper and contrast a fictional diary with an imagined neurogenic red-flag pattern; no diagnosis from isolated symptoms.
units.assessment: Submit an annotated diary interpretation and differential with triggers for specialist evaluation.

units.title: Spinal dysraphism, neurogenic bladder, continence and transition
objectives: Relate neurologic lesion and urodynamic risk to preservation of upper-tract function.
Describe longitudinal co-management, continence goals, sexual health and transition planning.
Distinguish clinical reasoning from procedural competence and explain supervision requirements.
topics: Spina bifida; neurogenic bladder; urodynamic risk; renal surveillance; catheterization/continence concepts; reconstructive options; sexual health; adolescent transition.
units.casePractice: Use a linked, published case only for structured reasoning and privacy discussion; avoid carrying details into public notes beyond its existing publication.
units.assessment: Design a longitudinal surveillance/transition map with shared decision points; no procedure checklist as authorization.

units.title: Congenital reconstruction: hypospadias, exstrophy, cloaca and anorectal associations
objectives: Describe anatomy and diagnostic context for common congenital genital/lower tract anomalies.
Discuss reconstructive goals, timing concepts, complications and long-term outcome assessment, acknowledging variation among techniques.
Recognize associated anomalies and identify when a multidisciplinary team is needed.
topics: Hypospadias; penile skin/curvature; bladder and cloacal exstrophy; epispadias; cloacal/urogenital sinus anomalies; anorectal malformation associations; reconstruction outcomes.
units.casePractice: Compare published case-report description with guideline chapter; focus on anatomy, outcome and consent rather than copying figures.
units.assessment: Create a complication/outcome framework for a fictional reconstruction case and identify follow-up outcomes beyond initial technical success.

units.title: Differences of sex development, genetics and pediatric endocrinology
objectives: Outline an interdisciplinary initial assessment for atypical genital development, including urgent safety considerations.
Identify when bilateral nonpalpable testes or proximal hypospadias with cryptorchidism requires DSD evaluation.
Use respectful, inclusive, developmentally appropriate communication and explain shared decision principles.
topics: DSD classification; endocrine/genetic work-up concepts; multidisciplinary team; urgent neonatal considerations; consent, assent, family values and uncertainty; privacy.
units.casePractice: Use one actual published case in the linked open case collection to practise non-stigmatizing case discussion; do not infer an individual’s sex/gender identity from anatomy.
units.assessment: Structured multidisciplinary handoff using fictional case details, scored for completeness, uncertainty, consent and respectful terminology.

units.title: Scrotal and gonadal disorders: acute scrotum, undescended testis, tumors and varicocele
objectives: Recognize torsion as an emergency and explain why investigation must not create unsafe delay.
Apply guideline-based cryptorchidism referral, imaging and timing statements with gestational-age qualifiers.
Build a differential for pediatric testicular mass and adolescent varicocele without collapsing adult oncology rules into children.
topics: Acute scrotum/torsion; cryptorchidism and retractile testis; hydrocele; testicular tumor; adolescent varicocele; fertility considerations.
units.casePractice: Open case-reports include pediatric gonadal/renal presentations; treat these as rare illustrative reports, not prevalence estimates.
units.assessment: Timed differential/next-step exercise with emergency recognition rubric; explicitly explain that self-study does not authorize clinical practice.

units.title: Stones, kidney disease, transplant and pediatric GU oncology
objectives: Describe pediatric stone evaluation as a search for underlying metabolic/anatomic risks plus acute management decisions.
Summarize urologic considerations in kidney transplantation and chronic kidney disease using multidisciplinary framing.
Differentiate renal and GU tumor presentations and identify specialist oncology pathways.
topics: Nephrolithiasis; metabolic work-up; prevention; pediatric renal transplant; chronic renal disease; Wilms tumor; rhabdomyosarcoma; testicular tumors; tumor boards.
units.casePractice: Use linked Frontiers case reports about pediatric stones, renal masses and testicular tumor as critique prompts; no re-hosting of images.
units.assessment: Tumor/stones differential memo with age, labs, imaging and multidisciplinary questions separated from conclusions.

units.title: Pediatric imaging and diagnostic reasoning
objectives: Select imaging questions appropriate to ultrasound, VCUG, DMSA, MRI and diuretic renography without ordering from habit.
Interpret reports in clinical context and identify artifacts, limitations and radiation/sedation trade-offs.
Communicate uncertainty and integrate longitudinal function and symptoms.
topics: Ultrasound; VCUG; nuclear renography; DMSA; pediatric uroradiology; image review; radiation/sedation considerations; case-based interpretation.
units.casePractice: Use publicly accessible, properly de-identified case reports or CHOP teaching material via links; image-use rights must be reviewed individually.
units.assessment: Interpret a fictional multimodality packet and justify what cannot be inferred from imaging alone.

units.title: Urologic emergencies, trauma and perioperative care
objectives: Prioritize emergency differential and rapid escalation pathways for torsion, trauma, obstruction and infection.
Explain basic principles of age-appropriate perioperative analgesia, safety and multidisciplinary coordination.
Recognize adverse event prevention, communication and follow-up as part of care.
topics: Torsion; trauma to renal/bladder/urethra/testes; emergencies; perioperative pain; pediatric medication safety; complications; consent and safeguarding.
units.casePractice: Use emergency case discussions as observer-level exercises. Do not translate online demonstrations into independent intervention.
units.assessment: SBAR-style fictional emergency handoff scored on urgency, differential, communication and safe limits.

units.title: Operative techniques, laparoscopy/robotics and complication analysis
objectives: Compare open, endoscopic, laparoscopic and robotic approaches as knowledge domains, not a skills credential.
Identify case selection, anatomy, complication avoidance and outcomes discussed in educational recordings.
Explain supervision, simulation and local privileging as necessary prerequisites to operative care.
topics: Open reconstruction; endoscopy; laparoscopy; robotic surgery; ureteric reimplantation; pyeloplasty; complications; learning curves and outcomes.
units.casePractice: Critique public operative-education descriptions in text only; do not download surgical patient media or treat video viewing as procedural training.
units.assessment: Compare two approaches for a fictional anatomy scenario and state supervision/competence boundary.

units.title: Ethics, pain, consent, equity and the pediatric-family partnership
objectives: Apply child-centered communication, assent and guardian permission concepts to sensitive pediatric urology contexts.
Explain privacy, bias, access and psychosocial impact in chronic urologic conditions.
Recognize pain/safe prescribing and seek appropriate specialist guidance.
topics: Professionalism; ethics; pain; assent and consent; DSD sensitivity; sexual health; privacy; health equity; complications; family-centered care.
units.casePractice: Discuss linked case reports only in a privacy-conscious way; no patient-record access or identifying details copied.
units.assessment: Ethics reflection scored for respect, consent/assent, privacy, uncertainty and resource referral.

units.title: Scholarly activity, outcomes, quality improvement and lifelong learning
objectives: Distinguish clinical outcome, quality-improvement, health services and basic-science approaches.
Critique endpoints, confounding, generalizability and long-term outcome measures in pediatric urology reports.
Use board-domain guides as preparation references without treating curriculum self-assessment as formal certification.
topics: Study design; outcomes; research ethics; quality improvement; manuscript critique; complication reporting; longitudinal follow-up; continuing education.
units.casePractice: Read an open case report and identify selection bias, reporting limits and non-generalizability.
units.assessment: Critical appraisal worksheet and a 1-page QI question; no CME/board credit.

assignment.title: Integrated pediatric urology reasoning portfolio
deliverables: A 6–8 page evidence-mapped case analysis using one fictional vignette and one link-only published case report; clearly distinguish case facts from invented educational details.
A developmental/upper-tract imaging differential and a separate LUTD/neurogenic risk comparison.
A one-page family-centered decision discussion with uncertainty, referral, consent/assent and privacy considerations.
A two-page outcomes/QI proposal with a measurable question, endpoint rationale, limitations and a literature date check.

rubric.performanceAnchors: Strong: prioritized differential, emergency/red-flag recognition, qualifiers and referral boundaries; adequate: mostly complete with minor omissions; needs revision: overclaims diagnosis or misses urgent risk.

Strong: uses primary authoritative sources, dates recommendations, separates standards/options and limitations; adequate: citations present but some date/uncertainty gaps; needs revision: uncited or stale guidance treated as universal.
Strong: matches modality to question and notes limitations; adequate: reasonable selection with incomplete caveats; needs revision: claims imaging establishes diagnosis alone.
Strong: respectful language, assent/consent, safeguarding, no identifiable detail; adequate: minor omissions; needs revision: stigma, privacy breach or unsupported assumptions.
Strong: justified endpoint and clear limitations; adequate: reasonable proposal; needs revision: confuses procedure count with meaningful outcome or overgeneralizes a case report.

assignment.submissionNote: Assessment is formative only; no clinical competency, board-passing, credential or procedural skill is inferred.

assessment.formative: 10 original single-best-answer questions plus unit quiz/short case-based assignments; discuss rationales after attempting.
assessment.summative: Portfolio rubric above; learner target is 80% rubric-weighted and remediation on any safety-critical miss. This self-study threshold is not validated board prediction.
assessment.boardCognitivePreparation: Questions train recall, interpretation, risk framing, guideline use, reasoning, urgency recognition and professional boundaries. They are original—not ABU examination items—and do not claim predictive validity.

studyHours.plan: 24 weeks at about 6 hours/week total: approximately 144 planned self-study hours including 39.3 h verified specialty video, 0.6 h foundation video, 2.7 h methods/history supplement, ~60 h readings/notes, ~17 h formative questions/cases, ~20 h portfolio/review, and ~4.4 h flexible consolidation. This is a study plan, not an institutional or clinical training requirement.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine
mapping.name: Pediatric Urology Fellowships
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The official page describes an ACGME-accredited two-year fellowship: one year of clinical pediatric-urology training and one year of clinical/basic-science training. Listed experiences include outpatient clinic, complex reconstructions/ambulatory surgery, urodynamics, spina bifida and stone clinics, fetal treatment and pediatric oncology tumor board; weekly educational conferences/didactics. It gives an application preference for applicants completing urology residency, preferably ABU candidates. This public description is not a full syllabus, current clinical schedule or case-volume guarantee.

officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The official page describes an ACGME-accredited two-year fellowship: one year of clinical pediatric-urology training and one year of clinical/basic-science training. Listed experiences include outpatient clinic, complex reconstructions/ambulatory surgery, urodynamics, spina bifida and stone clinics, fetal treatment and pediatric oncology tumor board; weekly educational conferences/didactics. It gives an application preference for applicants completing urology residency, preferably ABU candidates. This public description is not a full syllabus, current clinical schedule or case-volume guarantee.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The exact packet describes one Johns Hopkins School of Medicine institutional clinical fellowship, not a generic specialty-directory category, combined fellowship, research-only postdoctoral category or non-physician supplement. No Harvard-affiliated variant is listed in this item packet; none is inferred. Johns Hopkins remains an exact institutional variant. Its public page describes both clinical and research/basic-science content, but the track is an ACGME-accredited clinical physician fellowship, not a separate research-only track.
sourceCaveats: The Johns Hopkins public fellowship page supports programme accreditation and a short narrative of its two years and rotations, but does not expose a complete public syllabus, exact didactic hours, eligible-case volumes or current fellow schedule.
The 2026 ACGME pediatric urology requirements are the current version, effective 2026-07-01; ACGME accreditation standards are not the same as ABU exam domains or institutional teaching content.

The ABU 2024 candidate handbook verifies a separate annual subspecialty exam and requirements but may be superseded. Confirm the current application-cycle handbook directly with the ABU. The ABU pediatric-urology page returned HTTP 403, so no inaccessible content was inferred.

EAU Paediatric Urology guideline reviewed on 2026-10-07 identifies itself as the 2026 edition. The AUA VUR page remains marked published 2010/amended 2017; use with date qualifier and current local guidance.

The PedsUroFLO homepage states sessions have been on hiatus since 2021-01-01 and historical videos do not confer CME. Its public index and playlist list recordings. Public playlist metadata provided runtimes, but direct individual video playback checks encountered platform HTTP 429/403. One known unavailable VUR video is excluded. Link availability can change; recheck prior to deployment.

YouTube and institutional teaching media remain third-party content. Public viewing is not a rehosting, modification or embedding license. practiceQuestions.stem: A well-appearing infant has antenatal hydronephrosis and is being assessed after birth. Which principle best guides the next step?

options.text: The prenatal finding alone establishes reflux and mandates surgery.
Interpret postnatal imaging and risk in clinical context; distinguish dilation from obstruction and use current guideline recommendations.
CT is mandatory for every antenatal dilation.
A single ultrasound definitively predicts renal function.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Antenatal UTD is a finding, not a diagnosis of a single cause. EAU guidance discusses assessment by risk and condition; imaging must be interpreted in context, not as proof of a specific lesion.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a boy with suspected cryptorchidism before referral, which statement aligns with AUA guidance?

options.text: Routine ultrasound should localize every nonpalpable testis before referral.
Do not order routine imaging before referral because it rarely changes decision-making.
Wait until puberty for referral.
Hormonal therapy is the standard first step.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUA recommends against pre-referral ultrasound or other imaging because studies rarely assist decision making; referral timing is a separate evidence-based step.

practiceQuestions.stem: An infant with a history of undescended testis still has no descent at six months corrected age. Which response is most consistent with the guideline?

options.text: Refer to an appropriate surgical specialist for timely evaluation.
Wait for routine school-age screening.
Obtain CT before referral.
Assume acquired ascent is impossible.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUA recommends referral when spontaneous descent has not occurred by six months corrected age and separately recommends referral for acquired cryptorchidism.

practiceQuestions.stem: A phenotypic male newborn has bilateral nonpalpable testes. What is the key safety principle?

options.text: Proceed with circumcision before assessment.
Immediately involve an appropriate specialist to evaluate for a possible DSD.
Reassure without assessment if external appearance is typical.
Use ultrasound as a definitive exclusion test.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUA gives a strong recommendation to promptly evaluate bilateral nonpalpable testes for DSD; this is not a situation for routine delay or presumptive reassurance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with VUR has recurrent febrile UTI and bladder-bowel symptoms. Which framework is best?

options.text: Treat the reflux grade alone as the complete risk model.
Integrate infection history, renal status, age, bladder-bowel dysfunction and family preferences; consult current guidance.
Assume continuous prophylaxis is always required for every grade.
Assume surgery is always required after one recurrence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Risk-sensitive management considers both recurrence/renal injury and treatment burdens; the AUA guideline describes multiple options and uncertainty, and EAU 2026 provides current update.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child presents with sudden acute scrotal pain and torsion is a serious possibility. Which principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Defer escalation until outpatient imaging is convenient.
Treat as a pediatric urologic emergency; diagnostic imaging should not create unsafe delay in urgent management.
Use analgesic response to rule out torsion.
Assume torsion cannot occur in childhood.

practiceQuestions.rationale: EAU describes acute scrotum as an emergency; ultrasound may help but must not delay urgent intervention when torsion is suspected. Exact bedside decisions require clinicians and local pathways.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with daytime wetting and constipation has no neurologic red flags. Which first evaluation tool is emphasized in an open review of pediatric LUTD?

options.text: A structured voiding diary alongside history/examination and appropriate basic tests.
Immediate invasive urodynamics for every child.
CT urography as the first test.
Diagnosis solely from the symptom label.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The open 2024 review emphasizes voiding diaries and clinical assessment; urodynamics are reserved for selected complex cases.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with hypospadias and undescended testis has more severe genital findings. What should the learner recognize?

options.text: The combination can raise concern for DSD and may warrant coordinated evaluation.
It proves a single chromosomal diagnosis.
No endocrine or genetics perspective is relevant.
Routine imaging alone excludes DSD.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUA recommends considering DSD with increasing severity of hypospadias plus cryptorchidism; it does not establish a specific diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why is a pyeloplasty not necessarily an adequate sole endpoint in an upper-tract outcome study?

options.text: A technical event may not capture patient-centered, functional or long-term renal outcomes.
Every pyeloplasty fails.
Only operative time is a valid outcome.
Long-term outcomes cannot be studied in children.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Outcome selection should align with clinical aims and account for function, symptoms and follow-up; the PedsUroFLO lecture explicitly critiques procedure-only endpoints, and the ACGME requires scholarly thinking.

practiceQuestions.stem: After watching an online robotic reconstruction lecture, what conclusion is justified?

options.text: The viewer is competent to operate independently.
Viewing supports conceptual learning but does not establish supervised procedural competence, privileges or board certification.
Online video replaces fellowship case requirements.
An independent website confers ACGME accreditation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME clinical training entails supervised clinical experiences and assessment; a public video cannot substitute for training, case experience, credentialing or certification.

title: Pediatric Vitreoretinal Surgery and Ocular Oncology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (post-ophthalmology residency and vitreoretinal surgery fellowship prerequisite per public programme listing)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency graduate or senior level with foundational general ophthalmology knowledge; public programme eligibility is independently determined by the institution.
The target listing says applicants should have completed ophthalmology residency and a two-year vitreoretinal surgery fellowship.
Comfort with pediatric examination, retinal anatomy, basic ocular oncology/genetics and evidence appraisal.
This open curriculum is not a pathway or substitute for fellowship admission, license, credentialing or supervised practice.
objectives: Interpret pediatric retinal and intraocular tumor problems using structured, uncertainty-aware reasoning.
Recognize urgent findings and formulate safe referral, imaging and multidisciplinary discussion plans.
Explain ROP classification/treatment evidence, retinoblastoma work-up/genetics and pediatric retinal detachment differentials.
Appraise evidence, document source date and distinguish public program facts from educational extrapolation.
Understand limits of video learning, patient-image rights and the difference between knowledge and procedural competence.

units.title: Clinical reasoning for pediatric vitreoretinal and tumor referral
objectives: Construct a prioritized differential for leukocoria, strabismus, reduced vision, retinal opacity or detachment.
Recognize when suspected intraocular tumor requires urgent specialist evaluation and avoid maneuvers that could disseminate tumor.
topics: Red-reflex triage; emergency escalation; safeguarding and family communication.
boardDomains: ABO broad clinical judgment; no separate fellowship examination identified.
units.casePractice: Fictional referral triage vignette; no diagnostic photos required.
units.assessment: One-page referral note plus rationale for urgency; rubric: red flags 40%, differential 30%, safe next step 30%.

units.title: Pediatric ophthalmic examination, anesthesia and documentation
objectives: Adapt examination to age/development and cooperation.
Select noninvasive imaging and recognize limits of examination under anesthesia (EUA).
topics: History, red reflex, fixation/acuity, alignment, anterior segment, dilated fundus; consent and peri-anesthetic team considerations.
boardDomains: ABO broad knowledge and clinical reasoning.
units.casePractice: Draw a workflow on a blank schematic, not patient chart.
units.assessment: Structured exam template; rubric: completeness 40%, sequence/safety 30%, uncertainty 30%.

units.title: Pediatric posterior-segment imaging and multimodal interpretation
objectives: Match OCT, widefield photography/angiography, ultrasound and MRI to a clinical question.
State artifacts, age constraints and uncertainty rather than overcall.
topics: OCT/OCTA limits, fluorescein angiography risks/benefits, RetCam documentation, A/B-scan, UBM, MRI for extraocular extension.
units.casePractice: Compare modality roles using public teaching references; do not download/rehost imagery.
units.assessment: Modality selection matrix; rubric: question-fit 40%, limits 30%, safety 30%.

units.title: Retinopathy of prematurity: screening, classification and follow-up
objectives: Explain zone, stage, plus disease and treatment-requiring disease at conceptual level.
Use timely screening/referral logic and follow-up responsibility.
topics: ICROP framework, screening workflow, anti-VEGF/laser context, regression/recurrence and long-term follow-up. Verify current local criteria; no self-treatment.
units.casePractice: Fictional premature infant timeline; explicitly avoid inventing an image-based diagnostic finding.
units.assessment: Build a follow-up safety net; rubric: classification concepts 35%, timely action 35%, handoff 30%.

units.title: Retinopathy of prematurity therapy and late sequelae
objectives: Compare principles and trade-offs of laser, anti-VEGF and surgery without providing treatment orders.
Recognize recurrence, detachment and systemic/visual follow-up issues.
topics: Historic trials as evidence context; disease-specific choice is individualized; late refractive error, amblyopia and retinal complications.
units.casePractice: Critical appraisal: compare 2020 talk to current local/authoritative guidance before citing practice.
units.assessment: Evidence table including date, population, comparator, outcome and uncertainty.

units.title: Retinoblastoma biology, hereditary risk and genetics
objectives: Explain RB1 two-hit model, heritable/nonheritable patterns and implications for relatives.
Plan genetic counseling referral and surveillance discussions in the appropriate team.
topics: Unilateral/bilateral disease, germline testing, family communication, second cancers and follow-up; no deterministic inference from laterality alone.
units.casePractice: Fictional pedigree with uncertain testing; distinguish somatic from germline.
units.assessment: Pedigree memo; rubric: inheritance 40%, counseling/referral 30%, uncertainty 30%.

units.title: Retinoblastoma assessment, classification and differential
objectives: Structure clinical work-up and distinguish intraocular from suspected extraocular disease.
Use accepted grouping/staging terms cautiously and specify system/version.
topics: Fundus documentation, ultrasonography/calcification, MRI for optic nerve/orbit/pineal assessment, pathology after enucleation, ICRB vs AJCC TNM. Avoid intraocular biopsy when tumor suspected.
units.casePractice: Use NCI source tables and an invented text-only scenario; do not assume diagnosis from a single sign.
units.assessment: Two-system staging concordance worksheet; rubric: data capture 40%, system accuracy 40%, limits 20%.

units.title: Retinoblastoma multidisciplinary management and survivorship
objectives: Summarize therapeutic families and intent, preserving life first and vision where appropriate.
Communicate multidisciplinary decisions, uncertainty and family psychosocial needs.
topics: Enucleation, systemic/intra-arterial/intravitreal chemotherapy, local cryo/laser/thermotherapy, radiation and recurrence; indications are risk-adapted, center-dependent, date-check NCI PDQ.
boardDomains: Clinical judgment; no doses or unsupervised procedural content.
units.casePractice: Treatment-goal decision map without patient-specific recommendation.
units.assessment: Tumor-board style written briefing; rubric: life-safety priority 35%, evidence 35%, family-centered communication 30%.

units.title: Pediatric retinal detachment and vitreoretinal pathology
objectives: Organize inherited/developmental, inflammatory, traumatic and exudative causes of pediatric retinal detachment.
Choose appropriate ancillary tests and refer urgently.
topics: ROP, FEVR, PFV, Coats disease, trauma, sickle cell proliferative retinopathy and syndromic disease; pediatric anatomy and amblyogenic risk.
boardDomains: Vitreoretinal knowledge; no surgical skill validation.
units.casePractice: Fictional case tree, text only; avoid attributing specific case volume to the program.
units.assessment: Differential-and-test plan; rubric: breadth 30%, discriminators 40%, safety 30%.

units.title: Pediatric vitreoretinal surgery principles and safety
objectives: Describe broad indications and risks of vitrectomy, buckle, laser and cryotherapy in pediatric disease.
Analyze consent, instrument/visualization constraints and postoperative surveillance conceptually.
topics: Lens-sparing vs lens-involving considerations; PVR, proliferative vitreoretinopathy, iatrogenic injury, anesthesia and informed consent.
boardDomains: Not a surgical curriculum substitute; no procedural authorization.
units.casePractice: Review linked surgical techniques only as theory; do not practice.
units.assessment: Risk analysis for hypothetical procedure plan; rubric: indication 30%, risks/alternatives 40%, follow-up 30%.

units.title: Other pediatric ocular tumors and masquerades
objectives: Generate differential for intraocular and orbital lesions and identify life-threatening mimics.

topics: Coats disease, PFV, retinocytoma, infection/inflammation, medulloepithelioma and metastatic/secondary lesions as differentials; distinguish educational clues from certainty.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, ethics, research and board-style integration
objectives: Appraise evidence and state limits, date/version and applicability.

assignment.title: Longitudinal fictional tumor-board and retina consult portfolio
assignment.description: Submit four fictional text-only cases: leukocoria/retinoblastoma referral; ROP follow-up coordination; pediatric retinal detachment differential; multidisciplinary tumor-management communication. topicGaps: 28.63 verified specialty-specific recorded hours remain below the 36-hour floor; planned scripts and estimated learner/recording time do not count.
No separate pediatric vitreoretinal/ocular oncology board examination or published exam blueprint was identified; ABO general ophthalmology domains are only broad parent-specialty context.

Dedicated pediatric retinal imaging coverage (widefield angiography, OCT/OCTA, ultrasound, MRI) remains sparse in verified free recordings; sources describe modalities but do not establish a full imaging course.

ROP screening and longitudinal follow-up content is limited to three verified ROP recordings; criteria are jurisdiction/date-sensitive. The inspected 2025 RANZCO guideline applies to Australia/New Zealand, not as a universal protocol.

Pediatric retinal detachment / FEVR content gains one verified 9:02 case video, but PFV, Coats, trauma, PVR, developmental disease and surgical decision-making remain under-taught by verified recordings.

Retinoblastoma classification/staging, genetics, survivorship, treatment evidence and other ocular oncology need more verified free long-form teaching; current NCI PDQ and reviews support learning but are readings, not video hours.
Procedural judgment, supervised case volume, EUA/OR skill, and clinician assessment cannot be replaced by public recordings or authored scripts.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Single target physician fellowship in packet. This is a dedicated clinical physician track, not the separate one-year Boston Children’s pediatric ophthalmology and adult strabismus fellowship (AUPO-approved per its own page), not a research-only role, not a generic directory category and not a non-physician supplement. The institutional affiliation is preserved as BCH/Harvard; no Johns Hopkins programme variant identified for this named course. The 2024 co-director-authored account calls it the first dedicated clinical pediatric retina fellowship, but that contextual article is not a source for accreditation status.
sourceCaveats: Official target fellowship page describes clinical practice, responsibilities and application prerequisites but does not publish a detailed syllabus, duration, ACGME accreditation, volumes or separate board exam.

sourceReferences.title: ACGME Ophthalmology Overview

sourceReferences.title: Pediatric Retinal Detachments

sourceReferences.title: Pediatric Retinal Detachment Associated With FEVR
sourceReferences.claimSupported: 2024 clinician-authored review describes FEVR developmental vascular biology, widefield angiography, family screening, and selected surgical case-series experience; small series is not a comparative trial or generalizable treatment rule.

sourceReferences.title: RetinaRounds™ 45: FEVR-associated TRD
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Episode page posted 2025-04-14 identifies the public 9:02 video as a single 13-year-old FEVR case with progressive exudative/tractional detachment; it supports case-context and direct video identity, not a general recommendation.

topicGaps: 28.63 verified specialty-specific recorded hours remain below the 36-hour floor; planned scripts and estimated learner/recording time do not count.
No separate pediatric vitreoretinal/ocular oncology board examination or published exam blueprint was identified; ABO general ophthalmology domains are only broad parent-specialty context.

Dedicated pediatric retinal imaging coverage (widefield angiography, OCT/OCTA, ultrasound, MRI) remains sparse in verified free recordings; sources describe modalities but do not establish a full imaging course.

ROP screening and longitudinal follow-up content is limited to three verified ROP recordings; criteria are jurisdiction/date-sensitive. The inspected 2025 RANZCO guideline applies to Australia/New Zealand, not as a universal protocol.

Pediatric retinal detachment / FEVR content gains one verified 9:02 case video, but PFV, Coats, trauma, PVR, developmental disease and surgical decision-making remain under-taught by verified recordings.

Retinoblastoma classification/staging, genetics, survivorship, treatment evidence and other ocular oncology need more verified free long-form teaching; current NCI PDQ and reviews support learning but are readings, not video hours.
Procedural judgment, supervised case volume, EUA/OR skill, and clinician assessment cannot be replaced by public recordings or authored scripts.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: An infant has a newly observed white pupillary reflex. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Routine photoscreening at the next well visit
Urgent ophthalmic evaluation with a careful tumor-aware work-up; avoid intraocular biopsy
Start amblyopia patching before diagnosis
Observe for spontaneous resolution

practiceQuestions.rationale: Leukocoria can signal retinoblastoma or other sight/life-threatening pathology. Prompt specialist assessment is needed; avoid biopsy of a suspected intraocular malignancy because of potential extraocular spread. This is a safety principle, not a specific patient-care directive.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes ABO certification relevant to this fellowship?

options.text: The fellowship grants ABO pediatric retina certification
ABO uses written and oral exams after accredited ophthalmology training; a separate pediatric retina/ocular oncology board exam is not identified
Fellowship completion automatically confers ABO eligibility
Ocular oncology is an ACGME residency

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABO publishes a general ophthalmology WQE and oral examination following accredited ophthalmology training. The fellowship page does not establish a separate board exam or accreditation claim.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with bilateral retinoblastoma and family history should prompt which additional consideration?

options.text: Assume the parent has the same tumor
Discuss germline RB1 evaluation/genetic counseling and family risk assessment
Order no family evaluation because the tumor is bilateral
Infer absence of heritable disease if imaging is normal

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hereditary retinoblastoma has implications for relatives and surveillance; testing/counseling and surveillance should be coordinated with genetics/oncology. Laterality alone does not establish every individual’s germline result.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the most appropriate role for MRI in suspected retinoblastoma work-up?

options.text: Replace all ophthalmic examination and ultrasound
Assess suspected optic nerve/orbital/extraocular extension and intracranial associated disease as part of specialist work-up
Confirm every small retinal tumor by biopsy
Determine germline status

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ and multidisciplinary practice describe imaging as part of disease evaluation, including extraocular and intracranial concerns; it does not replace clinical ophthalmic assessment or germline testing.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about ROP treatment lectures from 2020 is safest?

options.text: Their advice is automatically current and universal
Use them as learning material, then verify current screening/treatment criteria and local specialist protocols
Use lecture slides as independent authorization to treat
Ignore long-term follow-up after initial regression

practiceQuestions.rationale: Therapeutic practice and evidence evolve; the 2020 recording is dated. Verify current guidelines and local protocols. ROP needs timely longitudinal screening/follow-up.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is true about retinoblastoma treatment planning?

options.text: Maximize globe salvage regardless of life-threatening risk
Use multidisciplinary, risk-adapted planning prioritizing survival while balancing globe/vision preservation and late effects
External beam radiation is always first-line
Treatment can be selected from age alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ states treatment depends on intra/extraocular burden, laterality, germline status and vision potential; goals include disease eradication, vision preservation and reducing late sequelae.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is a responsible interpretation of a public surgical retina video?

options.text: It certifies competence after viewing
It can illustrate theory but does not replace supervised training, case experience or credentialing
It authorizes independent operation if the viewer passes a quiz
It can be re-hosted if publicly visible

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public access is not clinical training or reproduction permission. Surgical competence needs supervised clinical training; resources retain copyrights absent explicit license.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pediatric retinal detachment is found. Which approach is most appropriate educational reasoning?

options.text: Assume adult rhegmatogenous mechanism
Construct differential including developmental, inherited, ROP-related, exudative and traumatic causes; seek specialist evaluation
Do surgery without further examination
Assume Coats disease is pathognomonic

practiceQuestions.rationale: The program source lists diverse pediatric retinal conditions and pediatric detachment has broad etiologies; distinguish possibilities and tests rather than assert one cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the appropriate rule for using clinical images in assignments?

options.text: Copy images from a freely viewable page into a course deck
Link to authentic teaching resource, preserve its terms and citation requirements, and do not copy/rehost images without permission
Remove visible labels and call images de-identified
Create synthetic images as diagnostic truth

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view is not an image license. Link rather than redistribute unless explicit reuse terms permit; do not use patient records.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner views an asymmetrically abnormal red reflex in a child. What is the immediate educationally safe inference?

options.text: This proves retinoblastoma
It is abnormal and warrants comprehensive ophthalmic evaluation; differential remains open
It excludes cataract
No further evaluation is needed if visual behavior is normal

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO PPP describes asymmetric, dull/white or absent reflex as abnormal; it is a referral trigger, not a diagnosis.

topicGaps: No verified free video runtime could be established from public metadata. The 14 uniquely identified provider-page videos remain duration-unknown and are excluded from hours.

Public recordings do not verify full coverage of puberty disorders, primary amenorrhea, confidentiality, child abuse evaluation, detailed endocrinology, fertility preservation, research appraisal, clinical decision-making, or many surgical principles.

No verified free recordings or independent lecture runtimes meet the 36-hour floor. Original clip plans total 36 planned hours but count as zero until produced and measured.

New scripts teach foundational developmental interviewing, HMB reasoning, primary amenorrhea framing, prepubertal safeguarding, suppression counseling and pain reasoning; they do not replace full specialty lectures, supervised clinical exposure, detailed algorithms, or a complete 36-hour curriculum.

No newly discovered recording was added to the counted lecture ledger because exact runtime and qualifying free playback were not verified; all 14 original Children’s Colorado items remain unknown-duration and excluded.

boardNames: American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG) — primary obstetrics and gynecology certification
ABOG Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology (PAG) Focused Practice Designation (voluntary designation with examination; not a separate PAG subspecialty board certification)

boardStatus.meaning: ABOG lists PAG as a voluntary Focused Practice Designation and directs candidates to an examination bulletin. This is a practice-focus designation under ABOG continuing certification, not a new subspecialty board certificate and not completion of this fellowship. The fellowship itself does not grant board status.
boardStatus.currentBulletinStatus: The ABOG 2026 Focused Practice Designation Bulletin is listed by ABOG, but its content and the static eligibility page load dynamically and could not be read through stateless extraction. Verify current ABOG board certification, licensure, practice, CME and case-log eligibility directly in the live bulletin; no requirements are inferred here.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course does not confer ABOG certification, PAG designation, examination eligibility or credentialing. The ABOG PAG FPD is voluntary and exam-based; current detailed eligibility must be checked directly in the official 2026 bulletin. BCH publicly requires completion of an ACGME-accredited OB/GYN residency for its fellowship, plus LCME medical school graduation or valid ECFMG certificate; these are programme qualifications, not an online-course pathway.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital; Harvard Medical School academic teaching appointment; clinical rotations at Boston Children’s Hospital, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
officialProgrammes.name: Fellowship in Pediatric & Adolescent Gynecology
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: BCH describes a two-year physician fellowship with Harvard Medical School academic teaching appointment; individualized clinical rotations at BCH, BWH and Dana-Farber; continuity PAG clinic; multidisciplinary clinics in complex anomalies, DSD/gender identity, fertility preservation/oncofertility, family planning, teenage obstetric care and sexual abuse; research and teaching. Public page states completion of ACGME-accredited OB/GYN residency and LCME graduate or valid ECFMG certificate. No numerical clinical volume or complete didactic schedule is published. Packet’s BCH GME directory field explicitly says accreditation “No”; therefore classified as non-ACGME, not an ACGME-accredited PAG fellowship.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One physician clinical fellowship institution variant is included, preserving BCH and its Harvard Medical School academic appointment and BWH/DFCI rotation sites as disclosed institutional associations, not as separate fellowship programs. It is a real clinical physician fellowship, not a research-only postdoctoral track, a generic directory category, or a non-physician supplement. Current BCH GME directory page is official; the supplied packet reports the listing’s Accreditation No classification. No Johns Hopkins PAG programme variant was identified in the supplied packet; this item’s assigned official listing is Boston Children’s.
sourceCaveats: Independent unaffiliated self-study only. It does not replace MD/DO education, accredited residency/fellowship, supervised procedures or case volume, licensure, board eligibility, radiation/procedure authorization, or certification.

No claim of Harvard University, Boston Children’s, Brigham and Women’s, Dana-Farber, Johns Hopkins, ACGME, ABOG, ACOG, NASPAG or CDC affiliation, endorsement, accreditation or examination preparation guarantee.
No human clinical review was performed. Clinical information can change; verify current primary guidelines and local law before use.

Clinical source page dates: ACOG menstrual cycle opinion reaffirmed 2025; ACOG HMB opinion reaffirmed 2023 with correction notice; ACOG suppression consensus includes 2024 correction; CDC contraception MEC 2024; ACOG endometriosis CPG March 2026; CDC STI guidance pages last reviewed July 22, 2021.

No patient record, institutional clinical image, source video, proprietary examination question or gated content has been copied. All constructed cases/questions are educational and fictional where labeled.

Video durations are unknown for all 14 embedded videos; no runtime estimates or playlists are counted. YouTube stateless metadata extraction was blocked by anti-bot restrictions; login, cookies and bypasses were not attempted.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 15-year-old has not menstruated. Breast development began over 3 years ago. Which next step best reflects a structured primary amenorrhea evaluation?

options.text: Reassure because menstruation is always delayed until age 18
Take focused developmental/sexual/medical history and perform appropriate evaluation for pregnancy possibility, anatomy and endocrine causes
Assume MRKH and proceed directly to surgery
Order a full pelvic examination under anesthesia for every patient

practiceQuestions.rationale: The menstrual-cycle-as-vital-sign guidance says evaluation should be considered by age 15 or >3 years after thelarche. Evaluation must establish context and assess relevant anatomic/endocrine/pregnancy possibilities; no single diagnosis follows from timing alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 16-year-old presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and dizziness. Which feature is the immediate triage priority?

options.text: Whether a family member has polycystic ovary syndrome
Hemodynamic stability including vital signs/orthostatic assessment and severity of active bleeding
Routine pelvic ultrasonography before any clinical assessment
Whether a menstrual app has a symptom color code

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACOG recommends assessment of hemodynamic stability in acute HMB. Clinical instability or heavy active bleeding warrants urgent hospital-level evaluation; routine ultrasound is not the sole first step.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adolescent with HMB has low ferritin and a history of prolonged epistaxis and easy bruising. Which reasoning is best?

options.text: Assume anovulation excludes a bleeding disorder
Assess anemia/iron deficiency and endocrine causes while evaluating for bleeding disorder with hematology coordination when suspected
Order routine surgery before medical assessment
Reassure because bleeding disorders do not present at menarche

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACOG directs assessment for anemia including ferritin, endocrine causes, and bleeding disorders. A bleeding history raises suspicion and should prompt coordinated hematology evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 14-year-old seeks menstrual suppression and says amenorrhea is the only acceptable outcome. What is best counseling?

options.text: Promise every method will produce complete amenorrhea
Use shared, noncoercive decision making, review individualized benefits/risks using current U.S. MEC as appropriate, and set realistic expectations that complete amenorrhea may be difficult
Require routine pelvic examination before discussing any hormonal option
Select a method based on caregiver preference alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACOG recommends individualized, autonomy-respecting counseling, the MEC risk framework, and realistic expectations. Complete amenorrhea is not assured; routine pelvic examination is not needed for most hormonal prescriptions (insertion procedures differ).

practiceQuestions.stem: A prepubertal child has vulvar discharge and a genital examination is needed. Which plan best follows trauma-informed principles?

options.text: Routine speculum examination to exclude all causes
A focused external inspection by an experienced clinician; minimize discomfort and use specialist consultation/testing based on indication
Interpret any genital redness as proof of abuse
Collect invasive specimens before considering child comfort

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC notes evaluations should minimize pain/trauma and be conducted by experienced clinicians. Scope and specimens depend on history and indication; findings alone do not establish abuse.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 13-year-old with disabling dysmenorrhea has no abnormality on initial ultrasound. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Endometriosis is excluded
Normal imaging does not by itself settle the diagnosis; consider endometriosis in the differential and apply current diagnostic guidance and shared follow-up
Immediate laparoscopy is mandatory in all cases
Pain is behavioral if imaging is normal

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 ACOG endometriosis guideline applies to adolescents and addresses clinical, imaging, and surgical assessment. Imaging has limitations; assessment should be individualized and avoid dismissive certainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adolescent with acute unilateral pelvic pain and an adnexal mass has preserved Doppler flow. What is safest?

options.text: Exclude ovarian torsion on Doppler alone
Maintain torsion in the differential and arrange urgent clinical assessment based on presentation
Recommend wait-and-see based only on flow
Diagnose endometriosis definitively

practiceQuestions.rationale: Doppler flow alone does not safely exclude torsion. This is a time-sensitive clinical condition requiring clinician assessment; the educational question does not authorize treatment or surgery.

practiceQuestions.stem: A minor discloses sexual activity in a confidential interview. What is the best first communication practice?

options.text: Promise absolute secrecy regardless of safety or law
Explain confidentiality and its limits, provide private time, and verify jurisdiction-specific consent/reporting rules
Share all statements automatically with caregiver
Document nothing to protect privacy

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACOG advises explaining confidentiality scope and limits and providing private conversation time. Laws vary by jurisdiction; absolute confidentiality should not be promised.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has a test result for an organism that can be sexually transmitted. Which approach is most accurate?

options.text: The result alone conclusively determines the circumstances
Seek experienced child-abuse evaluation, interpret organism-specific exceptions, use appropriate validated testing/confirmation and follow reporting law
Treat presumptively before collecting indicated specimens in every case
Ignore all STI findings in prepubertal children

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC states the significance varies by organism; some infections strongly indicate abuse while exceptions exist. Specialist evaluation and careful test interpretation are needed; reporting duties vary across jurisdictions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a new cancer diagnosis is about to begin gonadotoxic treatment. What care-process principle matters?

options.text: Wait until treatment ends before discussing fertility
Offer timely fertility-preservation discussion/referral before treatment when feasible, coordinated with oncology and reproductive specialists
Guarantee a specific preservation outcome
Delay cancer care until all options are exhausted

practiceQuestions.rationale: Fertility-preservation consultation should occur early enough to discuss options before treatment where feasible. Choice and success depend on patient factors, cancer urgency, and available services; no outcome is guaranteed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A review of one hospital fellowship page lists individualized clinics and rotations. What can a learner conclude about clinical case volume?

options.text: Exact annual cases can be inferred from the range of clinics
No numerical case volume can be claimed unless the institution publishes it; the page describes opportunities/rotations only
Every fellow performs every procedure independently
The online course itself grants procedural competence

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BCH public description names broad clinical areas and individualized rotations but publishes no numerical volume or autonomous competence claim. Independent self-study cannot substitute for supervised training.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly characterizes the PAG credential landscape?

options.text: PAG has an independent ABMS subspecialty board certificate identical to fellowship completion
ABOG offers a voluntary PAG Focused Practice Designation with an examination; this is not a separate PAG subspecialty board certification and current eligibility is bulletin-dependent
Completion of the Boston fellowship guarantees ABOG eligibility
NASPAG membership certifies physicians

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOG explicitly lists PAG among voluntary Focused Practice Designations and points to a designation examinations bulletin. The static FAQ/eligibility pages are dynamically loaded; applicants must check the current bulletin directly.

title: Limb Loss Fellowship
level: Non-ACGME clinical physician fellowship (packet classification; programme-specific accreditation not independently verified)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Graduate-level PM&R/rehabilitation physician knowledge; the institutional fellowships themselves require prior/ongoing residency as described above, but this course does not impose or verify professional eligibility.
Basic anatomy, biomechanics, wound/vascular concepts, pain mechanisms, functional assessment and evidence appraisal.
Learners without clinical qualifications should use this as general education only and should not apply it to patient care.
objectives: Reason across the limb-loss rehabilitation continuum using patient-defined function, safety and team roles.
Apply current VA/DoD lower- and upper-limb guideline qualifiers and distinguish recommendation strength from certainty.
Develop a broad, appropriately qualified differential for residual-limb and phantom pain.
Discuss prosthetic and nonprosthetic assistive options in the context of goals and trade-offs.
Separate institutional fellowship curricula, accreditation, primary board certification and subspecialty certification.
Critically assess case reports, public teaching media and image-use rights.

units.title: Scope, epidemiology, etiology and the rehabilitation continuum
objectives: Distinguish acquired limb loss from congenital limb difference and limb salvage; relate etiology and level to goals without assuming a prosthesis is desired or appropriate.
Map the individual journey from pre-amputation counseling through acute care, preprosthetic care, fitting, training and lifelong follow-up.
Explain why a one-year institutional fellowship is not itself a national specialty board or accreditation status.
topics: Dysvascular, traumatic, oncologic, infectious and congenital contexts; level and laterality; patient goals; setting transitions; team roles; outcomes and access.
boardDomains: Rehabilitation systems, function and patient-centered care
units.casePractice: Compare the two official fellowship descriptions; use an openly published case report only as a source of questions, not outcome generalization.
units.assessment: One-page continuum map plus a 400-word comparison of institutional variants.

units.title: Pre-amputation assessment, shared goals and perioperative risk
objectives: Organize functional baseline and patient-priority assessment across mobility, ADLs, cognition, cardiopulmonary reserve, vision, sensation, home supports and comorbidities.
Identify when vascular, surgical, wound, oncology, infectious-disease or other input is needed; avoid prescribing an amputation level from a rehab-only vignette.
Set measurable goals with the person and team, separating wishes from feasibility and uncertainty.
topics: Prehabilitation; shared decision-making; etiology-specific context; amputation-level preservation; functional measures including AMP where appropriate; nutrition and psychosocial support; perioperative prevention.
units.casePractice: Fictional case: dysvascular non-healing wound versus urgent trauma pathway; state what information is missing and which decisions belong to surgical/vascular colleagues.
units.assessment: Structured assessment checklist scored for completeness, role boundaries and patient-centered framing.

units.title: Surgical reconstruction, level, wound healing and complications
objectives: Describe the rehabilitation consequences of residual-limb length, joint preservation, soft-tissue coverage and surgical complications without substituting for surgical planning.
Construct a differential for delayed wound healing, infection, ischemia, skin breakdown, heterotopic ossification and neuroma using history/exam and directed tests.
Interpret guideline uncertainty on choosing surgical procedures and distinguish an exposure rotation from operative competence.
topics: Wound monitoring; vascular and tissue-healing context; residual-limb shaping; trauma/oncology; TMR/RPNI overview; osseointegration overview; complications and referral pathways.
units.casePractice: Use Cureus published transtibial case as a critique prompt: distinguish case narrative from generalizable evidence and flag where direct clinical reassessment is necessary.
units.assessment: Differential table with red flags, appropriate team referral and certainty rating.

units.title: Early postoperative rehabilitation and residual-limb care
objectives: Explain goals of postoperative positioning, range-of-motion preservation, contracture prevention, edema/residual-limb management and safe mobility.
Compare rigid/removable dressing and early prosthetic approaches as context-dependent options, not one-size-fits-all instructions.
Identify skin/wound findings that pause progression and warrant clinical review.
topics: Pain and wound surveillance; positioning; desensitization only when clinically appropriate; edema and limb-volume change; transfers; wheelchair, fall and pressure-injury prevention; residual-limb protection.
units.casePractice: Case-practice timeline: propose the next assessment and team checks for a fictional post-op patient with new redness; no individualized treatment instruction.
units.assessment: Care-plan rubric: safety, sequencing, monitoring, and stop/escalation criteria.

units.title: Prosthetic prescription, candidacy and device selection
objectives: Use patient goals, anatomy, skin/wound state, comorbidity, cognition, strength, balance, environment and anticipated tasks to frame a prosthetic discussion.
Describe socket/interface, suspension, components and broad device categories; select shared-decision questions rather than imply a device guarantees function.
Interpret functional classification/outcome tools as aids, not promises of coverage, candidacy or performance.
topics: Transtibial/transfemoral; upper-limb levels and terminal devices; sockets and liners; microprocessor knees; activity-specific devices; nonuse and non-prosthetic alternatives; cost/access and maintenance.
units.casePractice: Compare a fictional unilateral transtibial and transradial goal set and list options with trade-offs without assuming prosthesis use.
units.assessment: Prescription rationale matrix scored on goals, risk/benefit, alternatives and follow-up.

units.title: Prosthetic training, gait, transfers and occupational function
objectives: Recognize training phases and key mobility/safety domains for lower-limb prosthesis users and upper-limb device users.
Plan progressive, supervised functional assessment and state why unsupervised procedural or gait instruction is not supplied by this course.
Integrate OT/PT, prosthetist and patient feedback to revise the plan when fit, skin, pain or fatigue issues occur.
topics: Donning/doffing; wear/skin monitoring; balance and gait assessment; transfers; ADLs; upper-limb control strategies; fall prevention; functional mobility; therapy setting and supervision.
units.casePractice: Watch assigned recording(s), then annotate one visible feature as educational observation; do not reproduce copyrighted frames or prescribe a real-person exercise.
units.assessment: Video-linked observation checklist with context, limitations and safe referral.

units.title: Pain: phantom, residual-limb, neuroma and musculoskeletal sources
objectives: Differentiate pain perceived in the absent limb from pain in residual tissues and secondary musculoskeletal pain; consider multiple simultaneous mechanisms.
Build a targeted differential including wound, infection, ischemia, neuroma, bony prominence/heterotopic ossification, socket/skin and proximal/contralateral overuse causes.
Explain uncertainty for analgesic/interventional and surgical options and use current guideline advice rather than single-study claims.
topics: History/exam; urgent causes; imaging indications; neuropathic/musculoskeletal assessment; mirror/graded motor approaches as evidence permits; medication/interventional/surgical referral; TMR/RPNI uncertainty.
units.casePractice: Review residual-limb pain imaging review link and Radiopaedia post-amputation osteomyelitis case; list differential/next questions; do not download images.
units.assessment: Pain differential and source-quality appraisal; rubric penalizes pathognomonic claims.

units.title: Upper-limb loss, limb difference and myoelectric/assistive strategies
objectives: Contrast upper- and lower-limb functional priorities, levels, myoelectric/body-powered options and adaptive strategies.
Use upper-limb VA/DoD guideline algorithms and phases to frame rehabilitation questions while respecting patient choice and changing goals.
Discuss congenital limb difference/adult and pediatric context without collapsing distinct institutional or board tracks.
topics: Upper-limb level/function; prosthesis versus task-specific aids; bimanual participation; skin/care; pediatric growth issues as scope-limited; psychosocial and vocational factors.
units.casePractice: Analyze an authentic case or public teaching resource with no images copied; contrast a device-centered and participation-centered plan.
units.assessment: Short case conference scored on goals, alternatives, and age/level qualifications.

units.title: Limb salvage, oncologic, trauma and military/civilian model systems
objectives: Explain how trauma, orthoplastic reconstruction, oncology and limb salvage pathways alter coordination and timing of rehabilitation.
Distinguish a rotation/observation, an institutional exposure and board-recognized training; do not infer case volumes or competence.
Compare civilian and military system structures as the institution pages describe them, without extrapolating universal outcome claims.
topics: Multidisciplinary surgical services; trauma; orthopedic oncology; limb reconstruction; TMR, Ewing-type techniques and osseointegration observation; Walter Reed collaboration; transition planning.
units.casePractice: Create a fictional MDT handoff for an oncology/trauma patient and identify unanswered questions; no procedural steps.
units.assessment: Handoff rubric: role clarity, questions, follow-up, uncertainty and patient goals.

units.title: Comorbidity, primary care, prevention and lifelong follow-up
objectives: Plan lifelong risk review for residual and intact limb health, diabetes/vascular risk, skin, cardiopulmonary fitness, medication and prosthesis fit.
Use primary-care module concepts from VA/DoD guidance to identify preventive follow-up and indications for specialist escalation.
Recognize that guideline recommendations serve clinical judgment and are not individualized care orders.
topics: Residual/contralateral limb protection; cardiometabolic health; weight/volume changes; skin monitoring; equipment maintenance; surveillance; prevention and primary care.
units.casePractice: Construct a fictional 12-month follow-up checklist with contingency branches; no real patient advice.
units.assessment: Checklist audit against guideline domains and referral triggers.

units.title: Psychosocial health, participation, work, adaptive sport and access
objectives: Screen for psychosocial distress, grief, depression/anxiety/PTSD risk and participation barriers with appropriate validated services/referrals.
Integrate OT, social work, peer/community resources, driving/vocational services, adaptive sport and patient-defined participation goals.
Evaluate access, affordability, transportation and technology barriers as part of the plan.
topics: Adjustment and body image; mental-health care; caregiver and peer support; community participation; work/school/driving; adaptive sport; equity and access; shared decisions.
units.casePractice: Use patient-perspective sections of ACRM recording as historical lived-experience material; separate durable concepts from 2020 pandemic policy discussion.
units.assessment: Reflective analysis and participation goal plan; no outcome guarantee.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, outcomes, scholarly practice and board-cognitive synthesis
objectives: Appraise guideline certainty, systematic reviews, narrative reviews, case reports, institutional websites and recording metadata as different evidence types.
Use an original vignette to synthesize functional assessment, differential, treatment options, outcome measurement and follow-up.
Explain the absence of a separate limb-loss examination and the limits of mapping content to general PM&R board competencies.
topics: 2025 lower-limb and 2022 upper-limb CPG; GRADE and recommendation strength; outcome measures; journal club; quality improvement; original MCQs; institutional curriculum versus national board.
units.casePractice: Critique one case report and one guideline recommendation; build a short evidence-to-decision memo.
units.assessment: Capstone: 10-minute oral case synthesis and evidence map; practice questions are educational, not validated predictors.

assignment.title: Continuum and institutional-variant map
assignment.instructions: Compare the Spaulding and Johns Hopkins official pages. Map shared and distinct programme features and the handoffs across care settings.

rubric.criterion: Exact programme separation and source fidelity

assignment.title: Residual-limb pain differential and escalation memo
assignment.instructions: Using a fictional prompt, list urgent findings to screen for, distinguish pain locations, propose differential and question-driven evaluation/referrals. No patient-directed treatment plan.

assignment.title: Prosthetic goals and trade-off discussion
assignment.instructions: Use a wholly fictional case to compare goals, device/assistive options and participation trade-offs. Do not assert eligibility or outcome.

assignment.title: Guideline and case-report appraisal
assignment.instructions: Compare one recommendation from the current VA/DoD CPG with a case report or narrative review. State evidence type, certainty, population and limits.

assignment.title: Interdisciplinary transition-of-care case synthesis
assignment.instructions: Synthesize a fictional case across acute, inpatient/outpatient rehabilitation and long-term follow-up; state responsible professionals and unknowns.
assignment.deliverable: 10-minute narrated slide outline or written handoff.

assessment.format: Original educational quizzes, written assignments and fictional-case synthesis; not official board questions, validated predictor, or clinical competency testing.

unitMap.text: Scope, epidemiology, etiology and the rehabilitation continuum
coveredTopics: Dysvascular, traumatic, oncologic, infectious and congenital contexts; level and laterality; patient goals; setting transitions; team roles; outcomes and access.

unitMap.text: Pre-amputation assessment, shared goals and perioperative risk
coveredTopics: Prehabilitation; shared decision-making; etiology-specific context; amputation-level preservation; functional measures including AMP where appropriate; nutrition and psychosocial support; perioperative prevention.

unitMap.text: Surgical reconstruction, level, wound healing and complications
coveredTopics: Wound monitoring; vascular and tissue-healing context; residual-limb shaping; trauma/oncology; TMR/RPNI overview; osseointegration overview; complications and referral pathways.

unitMap.text: Early postoperative rehabilitation and residual-limb care
coveredTopics: Pain and wound surveillance; positioning; desensitization only when clinically appropriate; edema and limb-volume change; transfers; wheelchair, fall and pressure-injury prevention; residual-limb protection.

unitMap.text: Prosthetic prescription, candidacy and device selection
coveredTopics: Transtibial/transfemoral; upper-limb levels and terminal devices; sockets and liners; microprocessor knees; activity-specific devices; nonuse and non-prosthetic alternatives; cost/access and maintenance.

unitMap.text: Prosthetic training, gait, transfers and occupational function
coveredTopics: Donning/doffing; wear/skin monitoring; balance and gait assessment; transfers; ADLs; upper-limb control strategies; fall prevention; functional mobility; therapy setting and supervision.

unitMap.text: Pain: phantom, residual-limb, neuroma and musculoskeletal sources
coveredTopics: History/exam; urgent causes; imaging indications; neuropathic/musculoskeletal assessment; mirror/graded motor approaches as evidence permits; medication/interventional/surgical referral; TMR/RPNI uncertainty.

unitMap.text: Upper-limb loss, limb difference and myoelectric/assistive strategies
coveredTopics: Upper-limb level/function; prosthesis versus task-specific aids; bimanual participation; skin/care; pediatric growth issues as scope-limited; psychosocial and vocational factors.

unitMap.text: Limb salvage, oncologic, trauma and military/civilian model systems
coveredTopics: Multidisciplinary surgical services; trauma; orthopedic oncology; limb reconstruction; TMR, Ewing-type techniques and osseointegration observation; Walter Reed collaboration; transition planning.

unitMap.text: Comorbidity, primary care, prevention and lifelong follow-up
coveredTopics: Residual/contralateral limb protection; cardiometabolic health; weight/volume changes; skin monitoring; equipment maintenance; surveillance; prevention and primary care.

unitMap.text: Psychosocial health, participation, work, adaptive sport and access
coveredTopics: Adjustment and body image; mental-health care; caregiver and peer support; community participation; work/school/driving; adaptive sport; equity and access; shared decisions.

unitMap.text: Evidence appraisal, outcomes, scholarly practice and board-cognitive synthesis
coveredTopics: 2025 lower-limb and 2022 upper-limb CPG; GRADE and recommendation strength; outcome measures; journal club; quality improvement; original MCQs; institutional curriculum versus national board.

topicGaps: The 36-hour floor residual is 30.1547 hours after counting 5.8453 unique accessible free foundation-plus-specialty hours by observed duration; the 1.9297 hours of historical pandemic supplements remain excluded. Scripted episodes and clip target minutes do not count as rendered hours.

No verified free full-length lecture recording was found for many important domains, including pre-amputation evaluation and vascular/perfusion decisions, pain differential and diagnostic evaluation, wound/surgical complication management, primary-care prevention, pediatric limb difference, oncology/limb salvage, and formal outcomes/evidence synthesis. The new short recordings add only broad psychosocial discussion, an upper-limb overview, and a supervised-training demonstration; they do not close these topic gaps.

The original course’s source-based production plans and five new complete scripts are planned teaching assets only. They do not establish that the residual hours are produced, rendered, or available. The full 30.1547-hour verified-media gap remains.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.
