medical.programmeSourceScope: Verified 2026-10-07 from the official programme pages. These are actual post-residency clinical physician fellowship offerings, not merely generic directory categories and not research-only postdocs. Both pages describe clinical rotations and didactic/scholarly work. The supplied packet calls the track non-ACGME. Neither programme page claims ACGME accreditation for the limb-loss fellowship. The ACGME public-search page could be read but its search returned no program rows and did not permit reliable institution-specific query verification; current programme-specific accreditation status is therefore recorded as unconfirmed, not disproven. Their Walter Reed associations are institutionally distinct; do not infer a single joint fellowship.
sourceCaveats: Course is independent self-study, not affiliated with Harvard, Johns Hopkins, Spaulding, MGB, Walter Reed, ABPMR, ACGME or VA/DoD; no accreditation, licensure, board eligibility, certification, clinical privileges, procedure competence or guarantee of board passage.
No human clinical review has been performed.

The Spaulding page includes rotating clinical work, OR observation and research/scholarly activity; program listed in packet as non-ACGME. ACGME public search could not establish current negative accreditation status.
ABPMR has seven subspecialty certifications and does not list limb-loss medicine separately; no separate limb-loss board examination was verified.

The official pages describe clinical physician fellowships, not research-only postdoctoral roles or generic directory categories. Johns Hopkins is a distinct offering and retained as a separate institutional variant.
The two ACRM videos are pandemic-era supplementary media; policy statements are historical, not current advice.

PMC page extraction for selected 2016 and 2025 case-related papers encountered a public challenge; linked metadata was available through search, but full text or exact article reuse permissions were not verified.
Radiopaedia cases are link-only. If any image/text is later reused, verify case-specific attribution and CC BY-NC-SA/noncommercial obligations; public view is not permission to rehost.

Recorded-video totals are observed runtimes from unique YouTube IDs on 2026-10-07. Category-specific: foundation 1.0778 h, specialty 1.5803 h, historical supplement 1.9297 h. Unknown-duration public links are not counted.
Clinical practice, referral, emergency assessment, device selection and any treatment must be determined by appropriately qualified clinicians using current references and individual examination.
Fictional cases/questions are educational constructs. Published case reports are not typical outcomes; no patient record or image is copied.

topicGaps: The 36-hour floor residual is 30.1547 hours after counting 5.8453 unique accessible free foundation-plus-specialty hours by observed duration; the 1.9297 hours of historical pandemic supplements remain excluded. Scripted episodes and clip target minutes do not count as rendered hours.

No verified free full-length lecture recording was found for many important domains, including pre-amputation evaluation and vascular/perfusion decisions, pain differential and diagnostic evaluation, wound/surgical complication management, primary-care prevention, pediatric limb difference, oncology/limb salvage, and formal outcomes/evidence synthesis. The new short recordings add only broad psychosocial discussion, an upper-limb overview, and a supervised-training demonstration; they do not close these topic gaps.

The original course’s source-based production plans and five new complete scripts are planned teaching assets only. They do not establish that the residual hours are produced, rendered, or available. The full 30.1547-hour verified-media gap remains.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional person considering lower-limb amputation asks whether one surgical procedure is proven superior for rehabilitation outcomes. Which response is most consistent with the 2024 VA/DoD lower-limb guideline?

options.text: A specific technique is recommended for every patient.
The guideline found insufficient evidence to recommend one surgical amputation procedure over another.
TMR is mandatory in every case.
Prosthetic candidacy alone determines surgical level.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Recommendation 1 states insufficient evidence to recommend one surgical amputation procedure over another. This does not negate individualized surgical judgment or other considerations.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees new focal residual-limb pain after a socket change. No wound, vascular, neurologic or systemic information is supplied. What is the best reasoning step?

options.text: Label it a neuroma based on the timing.
Assume phantom limb pain because amputation is present.
Clarify symptoms and examine the limb, skin, device fit and function; screen for urgent causes before narrowing the differential.
Order MRI in every case.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Multiple causes can coexist. History and examination establish urgency and a question-driven differential; no single test or diagnosis follows from this sparse vignette.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient describes pain perceived in the missing foot while also having socket-edge tenderness. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Both descriptions can coexist and should be characterized separately.
Socket tenderness proves phantom limb pain.
Pain in a missing part excludes residual tissue pain.
All post-amputation pain is neuropathic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pain perceived in the absent portion is distinct from residual-limb tissue pain, but multiple pain mechanisms may coexist; characterize location and features rather than forcing a single label.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which interpretation matches the VA/DoD 2024 lower-limb recommendation on TMR or other peripheral nerve surgery for phantom limb pain?

options.text: Strong recommendation for routine use.
Strong recommendation against use.
Insufficient evidence to recommend for or against.
Proof that TMR is ineffective.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline’s wording is neutral uncertainty, not a universal recommendation or evidence of ineffectiveness. Individual surgical decisions require qualified team discussion.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most appropriate description of the 2024 VA/DoD guideline statement regarding osseointegration?

options.text: It suggests osseointegration as an option to improve prosthesis use for eligible patients with transfemoral amputation.
It recommends osseointegration for every amputation level.
It establishes universal candidacy independent of risks.
It is a guarantee of prosthesis use.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline gives a weak-for suggestion as an option for patients with transfemoral amputation who meet eligibility criteria. It is not universal or a guarantee.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician is reading a single published transtibial amputation case report. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: Its timeline proves expected recovery for all patients.
It can generate questions and illustrate one reported course, but cannot alone define standard practice or prognosis.
It substitutes for guideline review.
It establishes causal efficacy of all reported interventions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: An individual case report is authentic clinical material but provides very low-level evidence and cannot establish a typical outcome or treatment effect.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which accurately describes ABPMR’s current PM&R subspecialty certification list as accessed 2026-10-07?

options.text: Limb-loss rehabilitation is a separate ABPMR subspecialty examination.
ABPMR lists seven subspecialties; limb loss/amputee medicine is not listed as a separate certification.
Completing a one-year fellowship automatically grants a subspecialty board.
A directory listing establishes board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official ABPMR overview lists seven certifications (including BIM, HPM, neuromuscular, pain, PRM, SCIM and sports), not limb-loss medicine. A fellowship is not a board exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: The Spaulding page describes a two-month Walter Reed rotation, while the Johns Hopkins page separately describes a fellowship with Walter Reed. How should a curriculum catalogue represent them?

options.text: Merge them as one joint nationally accredited program.
Preserve the separate institutional offerings and accurately describe each page’s structure.
Treat Walter Reed as a board certification.
Assume all rotations are interchangeable.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The pages describe two institution-specific offerings. Shared partner exposure does not establish a single combined program or interchangeable curriculum.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee finds a public Radiopaedia post-amputation case image. What is the safest course-design action before using that image in an online course?

options.text: Copy it because public viewing means unrestricted reuse.
Link to the case for study and verify license, attribution, noncommercial and share-alike terms before any reuse; do not rehost by default.
Crop out the watermark.
Assume attribution alone clears every use.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia describes CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 conditions. Free-to-view is not unrestricted permission; linking avoids copying, and reuse must satisfy terms.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best characterizes the clinical training role of the Spaulding Limb Loss Fellowship page?

options.text: It describes a 12-month physician fellowship requiring completed or ongoing ACGME-accredited PM&R residency, but the page does not claim this fellowship itself is ACGME-accredited.
The page proves independent board eligibility.
It is a generic professional directory category only.
It is a non-physician research postdoc with no clinical rotations.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The page states 12-month clinical fellowship, applicant residency prerequisite, multidisciplinary clinics and a Walter Reed rotation. A prerequisite is not evidence of the fellowship’s own accreditation.

title: Limb Preservation and Wound Care Fellowship
level: Clinical physician and podiatric surgical fellowship; institutional 12-month non-standard postgraduate clinical training (not a residency specialty)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced postgraduate self-study for licensed physicians, residents/fellows, podiatric physicians/surgeons and allied members of limb-preservation teams; not a clinical credential.
prerequisites.knowledge: Foundational anatomy/physiology, diabetes and vascular disease, infection principles, wound documentation, evidence appraisal, and familiarity with multidisciplinary care.
prerequisites.clinicalSkills: This course supplies no hands-on skill sign-off. Monofilament examination, Doppler/perfusion testing, debridement, biopsy, casting/offloading, surgery, imaging acquisition or interpretation, and patient management require appropriate training, supervision and local privileges.
prerequisites.sequence: Review Units 1–4 and current IWGDF practical/prevention/PAD documents before case seminars; complete infection/Charcot and pressure classification before treatment-planning units.

objectives: Reconcile fellowship, accreditation, specialty directory and board-exam terminology using institutional and certifier sources.

assignment.title: Integrated limb-threat case conference and evidence brief
assignment.instructions: Use the fictional scenario: an adult with diabetes, a plantar forefoot ulcer of several weeks, rest pain, and a dusky toe. Key measurements, infection signs, imaging and patient preferences are intentionally omitted. Write a 1,200–1,500 word reasoning brief that identifies missing information; distinguishes PAD/CLTI from infection and Charcot mimics; proposes the appropriate urgent specialist/referral and objective-assessment conversation; maps relevant WIfI elements using the published chart only when inputs are supplied; outlines infection and osteomyelitis evidence needed without prescribing a patient-specific regimen; and ends with a team-based patient-goal/remission pathway. Use at least three current primary guidelines plus one institutional/certification source. Cite dates, label unknowns and include no real patient information or copied clinical images.
assignment.passingInterpretation: Educational feedback only. Not a validated board predictor, competency assessment, clinical credential or guarantee of passing any examination.

unitMap.text: Clinical frame, fellowship scope, and limb-preservation outcomes
coveredTopics: Hopkins program states one-year subspecialty training; directory lists accrediting body ‘Non-Standard’; public curriculum names interprofessional teams and gait laboratory.
Outcomes and risks; shared decisions, informed preferences, equity and goals of care.

unitMap.text: Wound biology, healing phases, assessment language, and measurement
coveredTopics: Normal/impaired healing; perfusion, neuropathy, pressure, moisture, infection, nutrition, medication, smoking and social determinants.
Wound documentation; measurement reliability; quality and recurrence.
Expansion: compare AHRQ wound-assessment/classification teaching with the current linked NPIAP definition; do not apply pressure stages until pressure etiology is established.

unitMap.text: Neuropathy, diabetes-foot screening, and ulcer classification
coveredTopics: Monofilament/vibration and vascular screening concepts (instruction is not observed competency); deformity, callus, skin, footwear, risk categories.
IWGDF prevention and classification; no single scale is universal.

unitMap.text: Perfusion assessment, PAD, CLTI and limb-threat staging
coveredTopics: History, pulses, ABI limitations, toe pressure/TBI, Doppler waveforms, TcPO2/skin-perfusion testing; imaging by trained teams.
CLTI, WIfI, revascularization planning, cardiovascular risk and shared decisions.

unitMap.text: Diabetic foot infection, cultures, osteomyelitis, and source control
coveredTopics: IWGDF/IDSA infection grades; alternative causes of warmth/redness including Charcot, trauma, thrombosis and venous disease.
Tissue versus swab culture; bone culture; imaging; empiric stewardship; source control; admission/referral.

unitMap.text: Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy, deformity, and infection mimicry
coveredTopics: IWGDF Charcot guideline; rocker-bottom deformity; active Charcot vs infection; offloading and monitoring; published cases.

unitMap.text: Pressure injury, device injury, and tissue protection
coveredTopics: Pressure/shear/microclimate/perfusion; staging boundaries; darkly pigmented skin considerations; device-related and mucosal injury.
Expansion: AHRQ pressure-injury assessment, device injury, wound classification and risk-planning recordings complement—not supersede—NPIAP terminology; AHRQ videos are historical.

unitMap.text: Venous, edema-related, arterial and atypical lower-limb wounds
coveredTopics: Chronic venous disease; arterial ischemia; mixed etiology; edema/lymphedema; inflammatory, malignant, traumatic and medication-related mimics.

unitMap.text: Offloading, footwear, gait, orthoses, and recurrence prevention
coveredTopics: IWGDF offloading guideline; non-removable knee-high devices when appropriate; contraindications/feasibility; gait and adherence; healed-ulcer recurrence.
Expansion: place the RNAO total-contact-casting discussion beside IWGDF 2023 recommendations and assess feasibility/safety; this is not a casting skills course.

unitMap.text: Debridement, dressings, wound-bed preparation and reconstruction principles
coveredTopics: Tissue viability; exudate/periwound; debridement indications/risks; closure options; offloading and vascular adequacy; documentation.

unitMap.text: Advanced wound interventions and evidence appraisal
coveredTopics: IWGDF wound-healing intervention recommendations; negative-pressure therapy for selected post-surgical wounds; topical oxygen, HBOT and skin substitutes evidence boundaries; regulatory status.

unitMap.text: Team pathways, clinical systems, quality, access and lifelong remission
coveredTopics: Hopkins public curriculum: collaboration with vascular fellows, wound nursing, home care, plastics, orthopaedics, rehabilitation and gait lab; curriculum limits; quality and equity; research literacy.
Expansion: AHRQ staffing and pressure-injury measurement videos provide general systems/quality examples only, not local benchmarks or a Hopkins rotation description.

topicGaps: 25.785556 verified free recording hours remain to reach the explicit 36-hour video floor; authored episodes and all originalClipPlan target minutes are scripts/plans, not rendered media, and count as zero video hours.

No verified free, directly accessible full-length specialist lecture was located for venous/mixed arterial-venous ulcer diagnosis and compression decision science; Charcot diagnostic/treatment reasoning; reconstructive surgery; or wound-intervention evidence appraisal. Current guidelines/reviews remain readings, not recordings.

Pressure-injury recording coverage improves etiology/staging boundaries, device injury, screening/risk tools, wound description, and systems but these AHRQ recordings date from 2015–2016 and do not replace current NPIAP definitions or diabetic-foot guidelines.

The new RNAO total-contact-casting webinar is educational and safety-oriented; it cannot teach or authorize casting. The 2023 IWGDF offloading guideline remains the current recommendation source in the packet; check for later guideline updates before clinical application.

No separate limb-preservation board examination blueprint or human clinical review was identified/performed. Board-domain references remain cognitive organization only; detailed undocumented Hopkins didactics/rotations are not inferred.

medical.boardStatus: No separate ABMS-recognized limb-preservation/wound-care specialty or subspecialty certificate, nor a distinct examination for the Johns Hopkins fellowship itself, was identified in the official sources checked 2026-10-07. ABWMS and ABWM offer separate credentials with their own eligibility rules; do not equate them with an ACGME-accredited fellowship or ABMS board certification. The Hopkins fellowship directory calls accreditation ‘Non-Standard’; an older/currently displayed Heart & Vascular overview letter says ‘fully accredited ACGME-equivalent’, a material terminology conflict. No ACGME approval was independently verified.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Johns Hopkins public curriculum lists prior pathways including general surgery, vascular surgery, plastic surgery, orthopaedic surgery or a three-year podiatric medicine and surgery residency, and states candidacy requires an ACGME-approved residency or CPME-approved three-year residency; it also says general-surgery residents may apply during research year(s). The directory and application pages do not resolve current year eligibility or licensure/work authorization details. Confirm directly with program and relevant credentialing bodies. Completion of this independent course confers no eligibility.

officialProgrammes.name: Limb Preservation and Wound Care Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official institutional listing: ‘Non-Standard’ accrediting body, one year; location/program director and multidisciplinary wound evaluation, surgical salvage and reconstruction. Johns Hopkins Heart & Vascular Institute overview/program curriculum is a companion official variant (12 months, post-residency pathways, surgical and wound core, case-log review every three months, gait analysis research and collaboration). The broader fellowship directory shows it beneath a generic Medicine search results category, not as a distinct ABMS/ACGME medical specialty. Its official program director is identified as DPM/podiatric surgery; vascular surgery faculty serve as associate program director. No second Harvard/Emory variant is in this packet.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exactly one official institutional programme variant supplied in the MED-185 packet (Johns Hopkins). Preserve institutional display name exactly. This is a clinical surgical/multidisciplinary fellowship, not a generic physician specialty directory category, research-only job, or separate board-certification program. The directory listing and overview letter conflict on accreditation wording; contemporary directory classification ‘Non-Standard’ is stated without upgrading it to ACGME approval.
sourceCaveats: The official Johns Hopkins program directory labels accreditation ‘Non-Standard’, while a linked institutional overview letter uses ‘fully accredited ACGME-equivalent’. This conflict is not independently resolved. No claim of ACGME accreditation is made.

The official application page still shows December 2024 deadlines; these are stale historical details and not a current application schedule. One fellow/year is public page description only, not an ongoing guarantee.

The medicine directory categorization is generic; fellowship leadership and curricular emphasis indicate surgical/multidisciplinary limb preservation. It is neither a board specialty nor an ACGME residency.

The page permits general surgery applicants during research years, but this does not transform the clinical fellowship into a research-only postdoc. Confirm individualized current eligibility with the institution.

Board credential pages describe independent ABWMS/ABWM credentials. Their organizations' use of ‘board certification’ is not the same as ABMS Member Board certification; review exact current eligibility with each organization.
As checked 2026-10-07, the IWGDF 2023 guideline hub says the guidelines will be updated in 2027. Recheck for new updates before use.
All clinical resources are educational; institutional/public sources may omit unpublished rotations, complete didactics, criteria, or protocol details.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with diabetes has a chronic plantar ulcer present for 3 weeks, new rest pain and gangrene at the toe. Which action is most appropriate in a learning vignette?

options.text: Treat only with a topical antimicrobial and review in 6 weeks.
Arrange urgent vascular specialist evaluation and objective perfusion testing while coordinating limb-threat care.
Assume the ulcer is neuropathic because the patient has diabetes.
Classify as unreconstructible without imaging.

practiceQuestions.rationale: PAD plus rest pain, gangrene, or lower-limb ulceration longer than 2 weeks meets the SVS description of CLTI; suspected CLTI warrants urgent vascular referral and objective hemodynamic testing. Etiology and treatment require full evaluation; the other options delay or overstate certainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: A neuropathic diabetic ulcer is present but there is no local or systemic sign of inflammation. In the absence of another indication, which infection-management principle is most accurate?

options.text: Give systemic antibiotics to accelerate closure.
Use topical antibiotics until the ulcer is fully epithelialized.
Do not treat a clinically uninfected ulcer with systemic or local antibiotics solely to prevent infection or promote healing.
Diagnose infection from a positive superficial swab alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IWGDF/IDSA explicitly recommends against antibiotic treatment of clinically uninfected ulcers for healing or prevention. Colonization alone does not equal clinical infection; reassess if signs emerge.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with diabetes and a foot ulcer has suspected osteomyelitis. Initial exam, plain radiographs and laboratory assessment leave the diagnosis uncertain. Which next imaging test is strongly recommended by IWGDF/IDSA when doubt remains?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
Routine CT angiography of the entire body.
No imaging because radiographs are always definitive.
A wound swab is equivalent to bone diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IWGDF/IDSA recommends MRI when osteomyelitis remains in doubt after clinical assessment, radiographs and laboratory findings. PET, leukocyte scintigraphy or SPECT may be alternatives in selected cases. A swab is not equivalent to bone sampling.

practiceQuestions.stem: A chronic heel wound is covered by dry, adherent, intact eschar without surrounding erythema or fluctuance in a patient with suspected ischemia. Which statement best reflects NPIAP guidance?

options.text: It must always be debrided to determine stage.
Stable eschar on the heel or ischemic limb should not be softened or removed under the pressure-injury staging guidance.
The wound is automatically stage 4.
It proves deep infection.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NPIAP says stable heel or ischemic-limb eschar should not be softened or removed. The appearance does not establish stage 4 or infection; clinical and perfusion assessment are needed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A superficial tissue injury is over a bony prominence following prolonged pressure and shear. Adipose is visible; fascia, muscle, tendon and bone are not exposed. Which NPIAP stage is most consistent with that description?

options.text: Stage 1.
Stage 2.
Stage 3.
Deep tissue pressure injury by definition.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Stage 3 is full-thickness skin loss with visible adipose; deeper structures are not exposed. Stage 2 is partial thickness with exposed dermis and no adipose. The description is hypothetical, and the pressure stage system does not apply to vascular, neuropathic, traumatic or moisture injuries.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with diabetes has a swollen, warm, erythematous neuropathic foot but no ulcer or systemic illness. What is the best reasoning step before labeling this as infection?

options.text: Consider acute Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy and other mimics while arranging appropriate assessment.
Warmth alone proves a diabetic foot infection.
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics in every case.
Use wound cultures despite no wound.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The IDSA/IWGDF infection classification requires clinical evidence of infection and notes conditions such as acute Charcot, trauma, gout, fracture, thrombosis or venous stasis can mimic inflammatory signs. A warm swollen neuropathic foot warrants prompt evaluation; this question does not prescribe care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A diabetic plantar forefoot ulcer has adequate perfusion assessment and no active infection. Which core management principle should be addressed early alongside wound care?

options.text: Offloading pressure from the ulcer using an approach matched to ulcer and patient factors.
Leave weight-bearing unchanged until a biologic is selected.
Apply compression without assessing arterial disease.
Use a dressing as a substitute for pressure redistribution.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Offloading is a foundational component of care for diabetes-related plantar ulcers. The selection must reflect location, infection/ischemia, adherence, safety and feasibility; guidelines do not authorize a one-size-fits-all device.

practiceQuestions.stem: A wound has failed to improve after standard local care. What is the best next educational approach?

options.text: Assume the wound is resistant and add every available adjunct.
Reassess diagnosis, perfusion, infection, pressure/offloading, systemic factors, measurement and patient goals before selecting an adjunct.
Increase antibiotic duration despite no infection.
Stop measuring the wound.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A stalled wound prompts renewed comprehensive evaluation of etiology and modifiable causes. Evidence-based adjuncts are selective and do not replace correction of ischemia, pressure, infection or other barriers; current guidelines and patient goals matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: An examiner documents a shallow open lesion on a neuropathic toe and labels it ‘pressure injury stage 2’ solely because the epidermis is missing. What is the key concern?

options.text: Pressure stages may be applied to any open wound based on depth alone.
NPIAP staging is for pressure injuries; neuropathic/vascular/traumatic and moisture wounds should not be mislabeled using that system.
Any wound on a toe is unstageable.
Stage 2 is defined by visible fat.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NPIAP explicitly cautions that pressure injury stages should not be used to describe non-pressure etiologies, including vascular, traumatic, neuropathic or dermatologic conditions. Establish etiology before classification.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes the Johns Hopkins Limb Preservation and Wound Care Fellowship and its credential implications, based on its public 2026-facing pages?

options.text: It is an ACGME-accredited residency with a dedicated ABMS limb preservation examination.
It is a 12-month clinical subspecialty fellowship listed as ‘Non-Standard’ by the Johns Hopkins directory; public sources do not identify a separate fellowship board exam.
It is research-only and has no clinical component.
Completion automatically qualifies every applicant for ABMS certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official Hopkins fellowship directory lists accrediting body ‘Non-Standard’ and duration one year; the institutional program page describes multidisciplinary clinical surgical training. No separate fellowship board exam is identified. Optional ABWMS/ABWM wound credentials are independent and eligibility-bound, not ABMS specialty boards or an automatic fellowship outcome.

assignment: Capstone: submit a fictional, source-cited interdisciplinary rehabilitation case conference brief with a functional formulation, prioritized data needs, a differential and safety screen, goal hierarchy, proposed outcome measures and limitations, systems/referral plan, and short oral defense. assessment.formative: Weekly self-checks, original MCQs, case formulation and evidence appraisal; discussion without patient information.
assessment.summative: Capstone brief + 8-minute oral reasoning exercise, scored 0–4 each: data acquisition, reasoning/differential, patient-centered management, systems/safety, communication/equity, evidence/caveats. Suggested pass threshold is a local course-design target only and is not a board standard or prediction.
assessment.rubric: Excellent: explicit uncertainty, relevant differential/safety, goals linked to function and preferences, proportionate evidence-based options, team/system coordination and respectful communication. Partial: gaps or weak rationale. Unsafe/insufficient: invented case facts, unsupported certainty, privacy/license breach, or treatment/procedural advice outside educational scope.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician residency curriculum (independent educational self-study; not a residency)
boardNames: American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR)
American Osteopathic Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (AOBPMR; parallel DO board pathway; details not independently sourced in this evidence set)
medical.boardStatus: PM&R is an actual physician specialty with primary certification. ABPMR specifies Part I written and Part II oral examinations after its required training pathway and unrestricted licensure. AOBPMR is a parallel osteopathic certifying board; current exact pathway details not independently verified here. A PM&R residency itself does not have a separate exam beyond the primary specialty board process. ABPMR lists subspecialty certifications as separate options; no fellowship is represented by this packet.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Only the certifying board determines individual eligibility. ABPMR describes four years of residency and Part I/Part II plus an unrestricted license. Self-study completion does not qualify a learner for any exam.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine
officialProgrammes.name: Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme outline describes PGY-2 through PGY-4 rotations and didactics: PGY-2 inpatient rehab (~9 months), outpatient MSK (~2 months), academic month; PGY-3 pediatric inpatient/outpatient, outpatient clinics, consultation/subacute/elective; PGY-4 outpatient/inpatient, brain injury, EDX, neuro/MSK clinics. At least four didactic hours/week and 12-month topic cycle. Local rotations listed are not an official complete curricular syllabus. Official page calls it a residency; current ACGME ADS program-level accreditation was not independently confirmed during this run.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One actual clinical physician residency in supplied packet. No Harvard programme variant, distinct combined residency, or pediatric-specific PM&R residency claimed. ACGME standard PM&R subspecialty fellowships and board subspecialty credentials are not silently merged into this primary residency. Research/faculty opportunities are not board-certifying physician tracks. No generic directory item or non-physician supplement counted.
sourceCaveats: Only primary Johns Hopkins residency variant is included from the supplied packet; no separate institutional variant or combined programme confirmed.
Official Hopkins page summarizes rotations and didactics but does not publish its entire lecture course or full private resident materials.

ACGME’s 2026 PM&R requirements allow 36 PM&R months following fundamental clinical skills in a separate programme or an integrated 48-month pathway; Hopkins advertises PGY2–PGY4 PM&R years. Do not misstate it as a three-year total physician residency.

ACGME-specific accreditation was not checked/confirmed in the public ACGME ADS record for this named program. The packet inclusion note says Hopkins directory labels residency results ‘ACGME Accredited or Equivalent’; that label alone is not treated as program-specific verification.

The Board’s exact eligibility determinations, examination weights may update; the Part I outline cited is the board-published outline effective starting in 2024. Verify current board pages before decisions.
AOBPMR was identified as a parallel osteopathic certifying body via ACGME/board result but its current pathway details were not independently verified in this source set.
No human clinical review performed. Clinical materials are educational; verify current guidance and consult qualified clinicians.

Public videos are selected records, not a comprehensive board review. The dated Johns Hopkins grand rounds video title/topic details are sparse; its runtime is verified but content domain coverage is not assumed.

options.text: Impairment
Activity
Participation restriction
Etiology

ABPMR Part I outline
MSKTC SCI factsheet

Increase exercise intensity
Wait for scheduled outpatient review

title: Spinal Cord Injury Medicine Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship / independent self-study curriculum-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Postgraduate physician-level academic review for learners already familiar with anatomy, neurophysiology, general medicine, neurologic examination, imaging fundamentals, and rehabilitation principles. Not an entry-to-practice or patient-care course.
recommendedPriorKnowledge: Medical school-level neuroanatomy and spinal pathways
Clinical examination and basic ISNCSCI terminology
prerequisites.learningSafety: Use only fictional practice cases or linked published resources; no patient-specific decision-making, examination/procedure authorization, or treatment advice. Learners must check current guidelines and local protocols.

objectives: Map SCI clinical reasoning to the published ABPMR outline while prioritizing its approximate traumatic/nontraumatic/unspecified etiology weights.
Explain mechanisms, level/completeness, serial neurologic assessment, and limits of outcome prediction using current standards.
Synthesize acute, rehabilitation, and lifelong SCI complications with explicit red flags and interdisciplinary/system considerations.
Interpret evidence and guideline currency, communicate uncertainty, and distinguish certification requirements from educational content.

units.title: Scope, epidemiology, mechanisms and cord systems
objectives: Differentiate traumatic, nontraumatic, and undetermined myelopathy presentations.
Explain primary injury and secondary injury mechanisms without overstating neuroprotection evidence.
topics: Applied spinal cord anatomy/physiology; injury mechanisms; SCIWORA terminology; prevention; epidemiology and risk factors; neural injury/regeneration basics
units.casePractice: Compare cord dysfunction mechanisms using the linked real pediatric SCIWORA case; do not infer a universal prognosis.
units.assessment: One-page mechanism map separating established clinical facts from hypotheses.

units.title: Neurologic examination, ISNCSCI/AIS and functional classification
objectives: Describe key sensory/motor and sacral examination concepts and AIS classification boundaries.
Identify common classification errors and the need for serial trained assessments.
topics: ISNCSCI; neurologic level; completeness; sacral sparing; AIS; reliability; SCIM/WISCI and functional measures; age-specific adaptation
units.casePractice: Use linked ISNCSCI worksheet as an educational reference only; no real patient examination is part of this course.
units.assessment: Classify a fully fictional vignette with itemized rationale; rubric emphasizes completeness and uncertainty.

units.title: Acute assessment, stabilization, imaging and surgical coordination
objectives: Organize acute evaluation around life-threatening associated injuries and evolving neurology.
Compare imaging roles and discuss decompression/hemodynamic evidence with guideline qualifiers.
topics: Trauma evaluation; spine precautions; neurogenic versus hemorrhagic shock; CT/MRI roles; acute consultation; stabilization/decompression; orthoses; prevention of secondary harm
boardDomains: Acute evaluation/management 5%; imaging 3%; spinal orthosis 2%; cardiovascular 5%
units.casePractice: Discuss the 2023 published pediatric case report as an imaging/definition question, not a treatment template.
units.assessment: Structured imaging-choice and escalation memo; no procedure steps.

units.title: Cardiovascular and autonomic emergencies
objectives: Distinguish neurogenic shock, orthostatic hypotension, and autonomic dysreflexia (AD) as different clinical problems.
Use a current institutional AD pathway and identify noxious triggers while escalating urgent care.
topics: Autonomic pathways; AD; orthostatic hypotension; spinal shock; cardiovascular complications; VTE/PE prevention and evidence updates
boardDomains: Cardiovascular 5% (spinal/neurogenic shock, OH, DVT/PE, AD, autonomic dysfunction)
units.casePractice: For a fictional change in baseline BP, identify AD as a safety concern, trigger evaluation, immediate escalation, and uncertainty; do not use a drug-specific protocol without current local guidance.
units.assessment: Two-column differential/safety plan, scored for hazard recognition, trigger reasoning, escalation and citation.

units.title: Respiratory, sleep, swallowing and communication
objectives: Relate neurologic level/function to respiratory risk without using level as a stand-alone predictor.
Identify surveillance domains for ventilation, secretion clearance, infection, dysphagia and sleep-disordered breathing.
topics: Restrictive impairment; respiratory muscle tests; ventilation and weaning; cough/secretion strategies; infection/aspiration/atelectasis; sleep; dysphagia; speech/communication
units.casePractice: Use published respiratory clinical practice reading; no copied patient data.
units.assessment: Create a respiratory complications differential and measurement plan with evidence citations.

units.title: Neurogenic bladder, upper tract health and urology
objectives: Compare bladder management options in terms of function, risks, preferences and upper tract safety.
Explain why symptoms/neurologic level alone may not reveal bladder pressure or renal risk.
topics: Neurogenic lower urinary tract; intermittent/indwelling catheterization; urodynamics; infection, stones, renal function; surveillance; AD interactions
units.casePractice: Compare source recommendations with a fictional patient-preference vignette; no specific treatment instructions.
units.assessment: Decision matrix requiring safety issue, patient preference, and guideline citation.

units.title: Neurogenic bowel, GI, sexuality and reproductive health
objectives: Differentiate broad bowel management considerations by neurologic pattern while avoiding rigid cookbook application.
Identify sexual/reproductive, pregnancy, swallowing and GI topics requiring team-based individualized care.
topics: Neurogenic bowel; dysphagia and upper-GI issues; sexuality; fertility and pregnancy; education and privacy
units.casePractice: Use linked public guideline resources and a fictional values/preference scenario; do not copy records.
units.assessment: Counseling outline scored for person-centered language, consent/privacy, referrals, and sources.

units.title: Skin integrity, pressure injuries, wounds and infection
objectives: Identify risk assessment and prevention principles and recognize infection as a competing diagnosis for deterioration.
Discuss wound staging and escalation without substituting a slide for direct clinical evaluation.
topics: Pressure injury prevention/staging; wheelchair/bed pressure; skin inspection; wound complications; sepsis/infection; latex allergy
units.casePractice: Analyze a fictional pressure-risk scenario; no wound image or copied patient image included.
units.assessment: Prevention and escalation checklist with scope limits and grading rubric.

units.title: Pain, spasticity, musculoskeletal and neurologic complications
objectives: Separate nociceptive, neuropathic and other pain phenotypes and use an evidence-aware differential.
Identify spasticity goals, bone/HO and late neurologic concerns for interdisciplinary review.
topics: Pain; spasticity; contracture; HO; osteoporosis/fracture; scoliosis/late spine; syrinx/tethered cord; peripheral nerve/TBI; thermoregulation/sweating
units.casePractice: Use symptom-pattern comparison; avoid asserting any single sign proves etiology.
units.assessment: Differential matrix with mechanism, red flags, source and uncertainty.

units.title: Function, mobility, seating, upper limb and assistive technology
objectives: Connect neurologic findings and person-defined goals to function without deterministic predictions.
Compare mobility, seating, adaptive equipment, upper limb preservation, exercise and participation domains.
topics: SCIM/WISCI; transfers, sitting, wheelchair and seating; gait/orthoses; ADLs; upper-limb preservation; FES/exercise; driving/accessibility; recreation/vocation
boardDomains: Functional assessment 2%; exercise/modalities 2%; mobility 3%; ADL 2%; participation 2%
units.casePractice: Patient/family educational materials may supplement clinical reasoning, not replace professional assessment.

units.title: Psychological health, aging, prevention and lifelong systems

unitMap.text: Scope, epidemiology, mechanisms and cord systems
coveredTopics: Applied spinal cord anatomy/physiology; injury mechanisms; SCIWORA terminology; prevention; epidemiology and risk factors; neural injury/regeneration basics

unitMap.text: Neurologic examination, ISNCSCI/AIS and functional classification
coveredTopics: ISNCSCI; neurologic level; completeness; sacral sparing; AIS; reliability; SCIM/WISCI and functional measures; age-specific adaptation

unitMap.text: Acute assessment, stabilization, imaging and surgical coordination
coveredTopics: Trauma evaluation; spine precautions; neurogenic versus hemorrhagic shock; CT/MRI roles; acute consultation; stabilization/decompression; orthoses; prevention of secondary harm

unitMap.text: Cardiovascular and autonomic emergencies
coveredTopics: Autonomic pathways; AD; orthostatic hypotension; spinal shock; cardiovascular complications; VTE/PE prevention and evidence updates

unitMap.text: Respiratory, sleep, swallowing and communication
coveredTopics: Restrictive impairment; respiratory muscle tests; ventilation and weaning; cough/secretion strategies; infection/aspiration/atelectasis; sleep; dysphagia; speech/communication

unitMap.text: Neurogenic bladder, upper tract health and urology
coveredTopics: Neurogenic lower urinary tract; intermittent/indwelling catheterization; urodynamics; infection, stones, renal function; surveillance; AD interactions

unitMap.text: Neurogenic bowel, GI, sexuality and reproductive health
coveredTopics: Neurogenic bowel; dysphagia and upper-GI issues; sexuality; fertility and pregnancy; education and privacy

unitMap.text: Skin integrity, pressure injuries, wounds and infection
coveredTopics: Pressure injury prevention/staging; wheelchair/bed pressure; skin inspection; wound complications; sepsis/infection; latex allergy

unitMap.text: Pain, spasticity, musculoskeletal and neurologic complications
coveredTopics: Pain; spasticity; contracture; HO; osteoporosis/fracture; scoliosis/late spine; syrinx/tethered cord; peripheral nerve/TBI; thermoregulation/sweating

unitMap.text: Function, mobility, seating, upper limb and assistive technology
coveredTopics: SCIM/WISCI; transfers, sitting, wheelchair and seating; gait/orthoses; ADLs; upper-limb preservation; FES/exercise; driving/accessibility; recreation/vocation

unitMap.text: Psychological health, aging, prevention and lifelong systems
coveredTopics: Depression/affect; substance-use disorders; cognitive issues; suicide prevention; aging; metabolic/cardiometabolic and endocrine health; nutrition; immunization/prevention; team systems; ethics and medico-legal issues

unitMap.text: Nontraumatic SCI, evidence appraisal and board-style integration
coveredTopics: Transverse myelitis, MS, spondylotic, tumor, epidural infection, vascular, metabolic/nutritional, hereditary/congenital, motor neuron, nonspecific myelopathy; research/statistics; ethics; systems integration

topicGaps: No verified long-form recording currently covers unit 2 (ISNCSCI/AIS classification, neurologic level and serial assessment); source-backed original explanation is scripted but requires review and production.

No verified long-form recording currently covers unit 3 (acute evaluation, imaging selection, stabilization and surgery evidence); the public 2026 Pitt agenda lists talks but no recording/player, so its PDFs are teaching slides rather than countable video.
No verified long-form recording covers unit 5 (respiratory assessment, ventilation, cough/secretions, sleep and swallowing); guideline and review readings are available but are not counted as video.

No runtime-verified open video covers unit 6 neurogenic bladder; a free webcast listing is registration-gated and lacks a public recording/runtime. The public PVA guideline and AAPM&R article remain readings, not counted video.

Units 1 and 12 remain thin for nontraumatic myelopathy (compressive, neoplastic, inflammatory, infectious, vascular, metabolic and hereditary causes), spinal anatomy/physiology, electrodiagnosis and evidence appraisal. Videos added mainly address lifelong complications, not full etiologic breadth.

Unit 4 is represented by the existing 86-minute autonomic lecture, but not by broad acute cardiovascular, VTE/PE and shock teaching. Units 7–11 gained recordings, though pediatric adaptation, guideline-current management, psychological disorders, clinical examination, functional assessment, and outcomes remain incomplete.

The verified free, duration-evidenced ledger is 14.3667 hours, leaving 21.6333 hours below the 36-hour video floor. The gap is real; authored scripts and future production estimates are not media and do not reduce it.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR) — Spinal Cord Injury Medicine (SCIM) subspecialty certification examination
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABPMR subspecialty certificate and exam exist; this is not a separate primary certifying board. ABPMR describes traumatic SCI and nontraumatic spinal cord dysfunction across ages. The examination outline assigns ~55% traumatic myelopathy, 25% nontraumatic, and 20% unspecified etiology. Current board page lists next SCIM exam October 26, 2027; this is date-sensitive.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: As checked 2026-10-07, ABPMR says applicants must hold current certification from an ABMS member board, a current unrestricted US/territories/Canada medical license, complete 12 months of ACGME-accredited SCIM fellowship, receive annual evaluation and program-director recommendation, and complete training by the August 31 preceding the exam. This self-study is not eligibility-granting.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This packet contains one physician clinical fellowship variant. Exact Spaulding/MGB wording is preserved above; affiliated clinical rotation sites are not misrepresented as separate fellowships. It is a clinical subspecialty, not merely a generic directory category, research-only postdoc, or non-physician supplement. The board recognizes SCIM certification through ABPMR; no separate primary board is implied. It includes nontraumatic cord dysfunction within board scope. Pediatric content is integrated because ABPMR SCIM covers all ages; no distinct pediatric SCIM fellowship/board track is asserted.
sourceCaveats: One counted public lecture was verified for exact runtime. AAPM&R/public health readings, patient education video libraries, ASIA purchased modules and videos with unverified runtimes were not counted as lectures/hours.
A genuine ready-media gap of 34.5667 hours remains. The planned original curriculum fills topics on paper only and is not rendered, recorded, uploaded, or ready video content.

The ACGME requirement document effective 2026-07-01 requires 12 months and at least three months each inpatient SCI rehabilitation and outpatient SCI medicine; this course cannot provide supervised experience, case load, or competency assessment.

The PVA acute guideline is an older edition; it contains legacy clinical language, so users must consult current living/local standards. The 2026 Outcomes CPG reflects literature available in 2025. Date-sensitive claims and board exam dates were checked 2026-10-07.
Human clinical review is not performed. No institutional affiliation, accredited training, licensure, eligibility, procedure competence, CME, certification or passing guarantee is claimed.

originalClipPlan.title: SCI Scope, Mechanisms and Etiologic Reasoning
objectives: Frame traumatic/nontraumatic/unspecified etiologies and injury mechanisms
Use examples to separate evidence from mechanistic hypotheses
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: A planned multi-clip module: anatomy and pathways; primary/secondary injury; traumatic mechanisms and SCIWORA terminology; nontraumatic myelopathy map; epidemiology, prevention, and source appraisal. Sum target duration includes planned lecture, retrieval practice and case discussion clips; needs SME review and media production.

originalClipPlan.title: ISNCSCI, AIS, Serial Assessment and Function
objectives: Explain ISNCSCI/AIS concepts and common boundaries
Discuss trained serial exam and prognostic uncertainty
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned short lecture sequence with licensed/permission-cleared worksheet walk-through, deidentified or fictional labeling exercise, reliability pitfalls, function measures, and feedback quiz. No real patient exam video.

originalClipPlan.title: Acute SCI Triage, Imaging and Surgical Evidence
objectives: Explain urgent assessment and differential for hypotension/deficit
Compare CT/MRI roles and evidence uncertainty around acute interventions
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned lecture plus expert case conference; imaging examples only from expressly licensed teaching repositories or link-outs; contemporaneous guideline comparison and no procedural instructions.

originalClipPlan.title: Autonomic Dysfunction, AD, OH and Cardiovascular Risk
objectives: Differentiate autonomic syndromes and recognize emergency escalation
Evaluate triggers and local protocols
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned case-based follow-up, not duplication of the counted UW lecture; AD safety algorithm, orthostatic hypotension differential, VTE and medication-review caveats with current-source validation.

originalClipPlan.title: Respiratory, Ventilation, Sleep and Swallowing
objectives: Recognize respiratory risk measurement and complications
Synthesize weaning, sleep and swallowing topics as guideline review
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned lectures on respiratory physiology, acute/chronic assessment, secretion management, ventilatory support, sleep and dysphagia with interprofessional perspectives.

originalClipPlan.title: Neurogenic Bladder and Upper Tract Safety
objectives: Compare management options with patient factors
Explain urodynamic and renal surveillance concepts
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned lecture set on physiology, options, infection/stone risks, urodynamics, shared decisions and current urology-source reconciliation; no catheter procedure training.

originalClipPlan.title: Neurogenic Bowel, Sexuality and Reproductive Health
objectives: Review bowel patterns and individualized management concepts
Address sexual/reproductive health with privacy and interprofessional care
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned evidence review and case discussion across bowel, upper GI, sexual function, fertility and pregnancy; clinician expert and lived-experience review needed.

originalClipPlan.title: Skin, Pressure Injury, Wounds and Infection
objectives: Describe prevention/risk and staging domains
Recognize infection and escalation issues
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned teaching with permission-cleared images only, staging limits, device/seating and skin checks, wound-care team roles, and infection differential.

originalClipPlan.title: Pain, Spasticity, Musculoskeletal and Late Neurologic Conditions
objectives: Classify pain domains without overconfidence
Map spasticity, HO, bone and late neurologic issues
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned modular series on pain phenotypes, goals of spasticity management, HO, bone health/fractures, syrinx/tethering, thermoregulation, and evidence limits.

originalClipPlan.title: Function, Mobility, Seating, Upper Limb and Participation
objectives: Connect functional assessment with personal goals
Survey mobility/ADL technology, exercise and participation
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned interdisciplinary case series on wheelchair/seating, transfers, mobility devices, upper limb preservation, FES/exercise and community participation.

originalClipPlan.title: Psychosocial Health, Lifelong Prevention and Care Systems
objectives: Integrate mental health, aging, metabolic health and social determinants
Design team-based transitions with accessible communication
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned patient-centered modules on depression/substance use/suicide, aging, preventive care, access, roles of the rehabilitation team, ethics and systems safety.

originalClipPlan.title: Nontraumatic Myelopathy, Evidence, Exam Integration and Board Outline
objectives: Synthesize nontraumatic etiology categories
Practice original questions mapped to approximate outline weights, with clear limits
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Planned case conference and evidence literacy series spanning compressive, infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic, vascular, degenerative, metabolic and hereditary causes; finish with original nonofficial questions and correction review.

topicGaps: No verified long-form recording currently covers unit 2 (ISNCSCI/AIS classification, neurologic level and serial assessment); source-backed original explanation is scripted but requires review and production.

No verified long-form recording currently covers unit 3 (acute evaluation, imaging selection, stabilization and surgery evidence); the public 2026 Pitt agenda lists talks but no recording/player, so its PDFs are teaching slides rather than countable video.
No verified long-form recording covers unit 5 (respiratory assessment, ventilation, cough/secretions, sleep and swallowing); guideline and review readings are available but are not counted as video.

No runtime-verified open video covers unit 6 neurogenic bladder; a free webcast listing is registration-gated and lacks a public recording/runtime. The public PVA guideline and AAPM&R article remain readings, not counted video.

Units 1 and 12 remain thin for nontraumatic myelopathy (compressive, neoplastic, inflammatory, infectious, vascular, metabolic and hereditary causes), spinal anatomy/physiology, electrodiagnosis and evidence appraisal. Videos added mainly address lifelong complications, not full etiologic breadth.

Unit 4 is represented by the existing 86-minute autonomic lecture, but not by broad acute cardiovascular, VTE/PE and shock teaching. Units 7–11 gained recordings, though pediatric adaptation, guideline-current management, psychological disorders, clinical examination, functional assessment, and outcomes remain incomplete.

The verified free, duration-evidenced ledger is 14.3667 hours, leaving 21.6333 hours below the 36-hour video floor. The gap is real; authored scripts and future production estimates are not media and do not reduce it.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fully fictional individual with known SCI develops sudden headache and sweating and has a blood pressure substantially above their documented baseline. Which response is most appropriate in principle?

options.text: Assume anxiety and wait until the next clinic visit.
Consider autonomic dysreflexia, activate the appropriate clinical pathway, and assess potential triggers with the treating team.
Diagnose infection without further assessment.
Use a generic online medication dose without clinical review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AD is a safety concern; assess urgency, individual baseline and potential triggers under current local guidance. This educational question does not provide a real-patient protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which distinction is most useful when initially comparing orthostatic hypotension with autonomic dysreflexia?

options.text: Use only the neurologic level.
Consider positional timing, symptom pattern and blood-pressure trend relative to the individual baseline; evaluate alternative causes.
The two terms are interchangeable.
A single normal reading excludes either condition.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The autonomic lecture discusses both conditions; clinical reasoning should incorporate position, timing, person-specific baseline, symptoms and differential rather than one variable alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reads a published pediatric case report describing SCI despite normal radiographs/CT and no appreciable MRI signal. What is the best teaching use of this case?

options.text: Copy its treatment regimen as current standard care.
Use it to discuss clinicoradiologic terminology and uncertainty; verify all management with current authoritative guidance.
Conclude normal imaging always excludes SCI.
Infer the same prognosis for every patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The linked case illustrates evolving SCIWORA terminology and a single published course; it is not a universal prognosis or contemporary treatment protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why is urodynamic assessment relevant in SCI bladder management?

options.text: Neurologic level and symptoms alone reliably show bladder pressure.
History, level and symptoms alone may not establish intravesical pressure, while upper-tract risk can be clinically important.
It is never relevant after SCI.
It determines board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The PVA bladder guideline explains that signs and symptoms alone cannot determine elevated bladder pressures and discusses urodynamics/upper tract assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of the PVA 2026 Outcomes Following Traumatic SCI CPG?

options.text: It proves outcomes can be predicted from AIS grade alone.
It recommends trained ISNCSCI assessment and serial monitoring but acknowledges variability and additional outcome influences.
It replaces clinician judgment and individualized care.
It applies only to one hospital's patients.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 guideline recommends thorough ISNCSCI, examiner training, algorithms, baseline/serial assessment and careful interpretation; it recognizes variability and factors beyond examination.

title: Spinal Cord Injury Medicine Fellowship Program
prerequisites: Graduate-level anatomy, neuroscience, physiology, clinical examination and evidence appraisal; designed for post-residency physicians or advanced health-professional learners as independent study only.
This is not an admission pathway; official fellowship application backgrounds listed by Kennedy Krieger must be checked directly.
No learner is presumed competent in neurological classification, examination, medication decisions, procedures or independent clinical care.
objectives: Apply 2019 ISNCSCI standards to classification data, sacral sparing, not-testable items and non-SCI confounders while documenting uncertainty.
Build differential and risk-based reasoning across traumatic and nontraumatic SCI and major secondary complications using current source versions.
Integrate rehabilitation goals, functional status, assistive technology, participation and interprofessional input without equating classroom learning with supervised practice.
Recognize high-risk patterns such as possible AD, VTE and respiratory compromise and explain appropriate urgent escalation principles without issuing individual orders.
Critically appraise board outline weights, guideline currency, institutional pages, case-resource rights and video availability.
Describe the distinct ABPMR SCIM exam and its published eligibility qualifiers accurately.

medical.family: Physical medicine, rehabilitation and sports medicine
boardNames: American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR) — Spinal Cord Injury Medicine (SCIM) subspecialty certification examination
ABMS member-board primary certification prerequisite (candidate-specific primary board; not conferred by this curriculum)
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABPMR SCIM subspecialty certification exam exists; ABPMR page lists the next exam for October 26, 2027. The SCIM course is not board preparation validation and cannot grant certification.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: As checked 2026-10-07, ABPMR says SCIM applicants need current certification by an ABMS member board, a current valid unrestricted US/territory/Canada medical license, 12 months of ACGME-accredited SCIM fellowship, annual program director evaluation and program director recommendation; training must finish after residency by the August 31 preceding the examination. Current program/application details govern. Kennedy Krieger posted application page separately lists physician applicants and ACGME residency backgrounds: anesthesiology, emergency medicine, family medicine, general surgery, internal medicine, neurology, neurological surgery, orthopedic surgery, pediatrics, PM&R, plastic surgery or urology. These are program-admission prerequisites, not a guarantee of exam eligibility.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, in partnership with Kennedy Krieger Institute
officialProgrammes.name: Spinal Cord Injury Medicine (SCIM) Fellowship Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Johns Hopkins directory names this exact program and marks it ACGME accredited, 1 year, location Johns Hopkins Hospital and Kennedy Krieger. Hopkins PM&R education page separately describes a one-year ACGME-accredited fellowship, total approved positions one, adult and pediatric acute/chronic traumatic and nontraumatic exposure, and clinical sites Kennedy Krieger, Johns Hopkins Hospital, Johns Hopkins Bayview and University of Maryland. Kennedy Krieger publishes an illustrative month-by-month rotation schedule and elective/subrotation list; it is an example, not guaranteed fellow experience or a complete internal curriculum.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One clinical physician subspecialty fellowship; not a residency, research-only postdoctoral job, nonphysician supplement or generic directory category. Institutional variants retained: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine directory label “Spinal Cord Injury Medicine (SCIM) Fellowship Program”; Hopkins PM&R page label “Spinal Cord Injury Fellowship”; Kennedy Krieger Institute program label “Spinal Cord Injury Medicine (SCIM) Fellowship Program.” Hopkins/KKI are partners in the same fellowship; no Harvard-affiliated offering identified in the supplied item scope. Not a combined-board program. The institution webpage calls it ACGME-accredited, confirmed by current public program pages; accreditation status is time sensitive.
sourceCaveats: ACGME requirements, board requirements, institutional recruitment details and clinical guidelines can change; check primary current source before use.
The public Kennedy Krieger rotation schedule is presented as an example. It cannot establish all fellows receive specific experience, volume, competence or outcome.
The ABPMR outline is an approximate content-weighting document, not a disclosed complete exam blueprint or exam questions.
Free-to-view sources do not automatically grant copying, download, embedding or redistribution rights. All case and video resources are linked, not copied.
AAPM&R focused review course is explicitly paywalled; excluded. No free recorded 36-hour SCIM-specific lecture series was verified.

All clinical content requires independent clinician review. Human clinical review was not performed. No diagnosis, patient-specific treatment order, case-volume representation or passing guarantee is made.

Exact duration observation: public YouTube player/card listed 1:26:24 for autonomic lecture and displayed 59:51 on primary-care lecture. Times are source-page readings; media were not locally downloaded/probed. Recheck availability and runtime before reuse.
No additional Harvard-associated SCIM fellowship is asserted from this packet; the item covers the one stated Johns Hopkins/Kennedy Krieger program.

The linked 2022 Cureus AD case report is a published case example, not a clinical guideline. Authors acknowledge patient consent; the source text reviewed here does not explicitly establish de-identification or rights to reuse figures. Link only and check current CPG before drawing clinical conclusions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A standardized worksheet has preserved light touch at S4-5 on one side, absent deep anal pressure, and absent voluntary anal contraction. Which interpretation is most defensible?

options.text: S4-5 sensory preservation must be ignored because DAP is absent
Sensory ZPP is not applicable on the side with preserved S4-5 sensation; apply the 2019 worksheet rules and assess each side separately
All sensory ZPPs are automatically absent
Classify AIS A solely from absent DAP

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2019 ISNCSCI rules make sensory ZPP not applicable on a side with preserved S4-5 LT or PP; sensory ZPPs may differ by side. Classification requires the full worksheet, not one finding.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult with a chronic SCI at T4 has an abrupt systolic blood-pressure rise 25 mmHg above their usual baseline and new headache. What is the best immediate cognitive response?

options.text: Assume a primary headache and wait for pain
Recognize possible AD, check BP and rapidly assess for triggers while initiating the guideline response and escalation appropriate to setting
Diagnose a urinary infection without testing
Treat as orthostatic hypotension

practiceQuestions.rationale: The PVA guideline identifies SCI at/above T6 and a systolic rise greater than 20 mmHg over baseline as consistent with AD; confirm blood pressure, address trigger, and use the guideline-based urgent response. This is an educational question, not an individual order.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician encounters a neurologic score impaired by a documented peripheral nerve injury. How should the score be handled for ISNCSCI classification?

options.text: Replace it with normal without documentation
Record the actual finding, document the non-SCI condition and follow 2019 tagging/interpretation rules; disclose any classification assumption
Exclude the entire exam
Assign AIS E

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2019 standards advise actual scores, tagging impaired scores affected by a non-SCI condition, comment documentation, and marking assumptions; classification components can be indeterminate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most accurate statement about the SCIM examination pathway described by ABPMR?

options.text: Any learner completing an online course is eligible
Candidates need current ABMS-member-board certification, a valid unrestricted license, and 12 months of ACGME-accredited SCIM fellowship plus program director recommendation/evaluation
A state license alone guarantees eligibility
The Hopkins program awards board certification

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPMR lists these eligibility elements. A self-study course does not satisfy fellowship, licensure or certification requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement matches the current posted Hopkins SCIM fellowship?

options.text: It is a research-only fellowship without clinical training
It is a one-year ACGME-accredited fellowship with adult and pediatric, acute and chronic, traumatic and nontraumatic SCI exposure
It is a generic directory category without an institutional program
It is a two-year combined spine-surgery/PM&R board pathway

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Johns Hopkins Medicine page describes a one-year ACGME-accredited fellowship offered with Kennedy Krieger and breadth across age and etiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is planning a public curriculum around the posted Hopkins program. What is the defensible use of Kennedy Krieger monthly rotation schedule?

options.text: Present it as guaranteed rotations every year for all fellows
Describe it as a publicly posted example schedule, and distinguish it from independently observed performance or guaranteed case volume
Claim that schedule alone meets every competency
Call each site a separate board certification

practiceQuestions.rationale: The source labels a rotation schedule example. It describes site/month organization but does not guarantee individual exposure or case volumes.

practiceQuestions.stem: A participant with chronic SCI reports shoulder pain during wheelchair propulsion. Which reasoning is best?

options.text: Assume neuropathic pain and prescribe one medication
Classify likely pain mechanisms and function, assess overuse/biomechanics and other causes, then coordinate a person-centered evaluation/referral
Assume the shoulder is unrelated to SCI
Recommend surgery without an assessment

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPMR domains and PVA pain/upper-limb guidance support a differential, functional assessment and interprofessional management; symptom description alone does not prove etiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which source is appropriate for practicing ISNCSCI with answer feedback while respecting rights?

options.text: Copy a patient MRI from a commercial site
Use the public ASIA workbook at its source, respect copyright, and do not assume reuse permission
Download identifiable clinical records from a hospital portal
Treat an invented image as a patient scan

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASIA provides a public worksheet/case workbook with educational cases; the public link is appropriate for learning, but rehosting rights were not established.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee cites an online lecture posted in 2017 about primary care screening after SCI as the sole current standard. What is the best scholarly response?

options.text: Accept it without review because the presenter is an expert
Use it as a historical/educational lecture and cross-check current prevention recommendations and local guidance before application
Delete all preventive care from curriculum
Assume recommendations never change

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public recorded lectures can be useful but date-sensitive screening must be cross-checked. The lecture itself is not an official current guideline.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with SCI has acute respiratory symptoms and impaired cough. Which course-level approach is sound?

options.text: Assume the neurological level alone establishes respiratory failure
Use clinical examination and current respiratory guidance to consider ventilatory/airway-clearance risk, infection and escalation; individual care requires supervised clinical judgment
Defer all assessment until the next annual visit
Use a consumer video as the sole management protocol

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME and PVA sources emphasize pulmonary complication competence. Actual assessment and management must be individualized by treating clinicians.

topicGaps: AMSSM lists 35 basic/13 advanced ultrasound modules as free but per-video durations were not observed, so none of those hours count.
Hands-on scanning, imaging acquisition, injections, fluoroscopic procedures and sideline care require supervised training; no competence can be acquired here.
Spaulding internal schedule, case volumes and complete didactics were not public on fetched page.
Local PPE/ECG workflow, current emergency action plan and patient-specific return-to-sport require current professional context.

Two additional accessible AMSSM recordings now add a focused CPET lecture and an exercise-prescription/chronic-disease lecture. Their runtime is counted; they do not establish a learner’s ability to perform testing or make a patient-specific prescription.

The IOC REDs CAT2 framework is now supported by an authored teaching episode, but risk scoring cannot independently diagnose REDs or determine participation; physician-led multidisciplinary assessment remains necessary.

AMSSM ultrasound module runtimes remain unobserved and excluded. Conceptual teaching and source-hosted cases cannot substitute for probe handling, image acquisition, interpretation under supervision, or procedural skills.

No episode can replace direct supervised patient care, event coverage, PPE practice, procedures, longitudinal follow-up, team-based clinical judgment, or the confidential site-specific emergency plans required in accredited fellowship.

Public source coverage is uneven for some blueprint areas (including current, setting-specific pathways for less common medical conditions and local legal/return-to-sport rules). Use current governing-body and institutional sources; gaps are not claims of absence from formal fellowships.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: A separate Sports Medicine certification examination exists. ABFM develops/administers the shared exam for several board pathways while boards determine eligibility/credentialing. ABPMR, ABFM, ABEM and ABP have Sports Medicine pathways; ABIM diplomates may qualify through the ABEM pathway subject to its rules. This is primary-care sports medicine, not the separate ABOS Orthopaedic Sports Medicine pathway.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course gives no board eligibility. Rules change and candidates must confirm with their board. Spaulding lists FM, IM, osteopathic neuromusculoskeletal medicine, pediatrics, and PM&R residencies for this fellowship; Emergency Medicine applicants are directed to a distinct Emergency Sports Medicine Fellowship. Board eligibility requires applicable primary certification, licensure, and completion/verification of accredited fellowship training; independent videos are not a substitute.

officialProgrammes.institution: Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Sports Medicine Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page identifies an ACGME-accredited physician fellowship and eligibility after FM/IM/osteopathic neuromusculoskeletal medicine/Pediatrics/PM&R residency. It describes four 3-month blocks with medical/orthopaedic sports medicine, pediatrics, hand, sports cardiology, MSK radiology, running medicine, ultrasound/procedures and electives, with weekly didactics and event coverage. Full weekly schedule, case counts and internal lecture set are not public on fetched page. EM applicants are directed to a separate fellowship.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One actual physician clinical fellowship, not a research-only postdoctoral position, generic directory category, or combined residency. The separate EM fellowship is not merged into this item; cross-board certification is not combined training.
sourceCaveats: The counted ledger consists only of 63 unique recordings in two public AMSSM annual Fellow Online Lecture playlists (2024-25 and 2025-26). Public listing shows 33 and 30 videos, respectively; runtimes were read from YouTube playlist pages and cross-checked with yt-dlp public flat-playlist metadata; no media downloaded.
Public free-to-view status was checked statelessly on 2026-10-07; availability can change and links should be rechecked. No mirroring or rehosting.
No AMSSM ultrasound didactic video time is counted: the official source states free access but individual runtimes were not observable. Optional CME packaging is paid.
Clinical/board sources date-checked 2026-10-07. ACSM 2023 full journal text may be paywalled; PubMed abstract is public. No paywall or authentication was bypassed.
Spaulding public page does not provide all internal didactics, case volume, detailed timetable, or evaluation outcomes.

No human clinical review. All written vignettes are fictional and questions are original, not official or leaked exam material. Authentic AMSSM case links are source-hosted and described as de-identified; no patient media or records reproduced.
